Introduction

This game system was inspired from the premise that Fire Emblem tactical combat mechanics would mix spectacularly well with DnD-style tabletop roleplaying. That is more or less the vision. While every TTRPG makes compromises between the tenuous balance of narrative and crunchy gameplay, I have always felt that Fire Emblem was unique in how, when done right, the map design and combat itself could dynamically tell a story all on its own without a shred of dialog or flashy cinematic cutscenes. FE Engage is not a good story (hot take I know), and yet... it has one of the most memorable and compelling story moments in any Fire Emblem I've ever played. Chapter 11. And if you've played it, especially on Hard or Maddening, you know exactly why.

Chapter 11 of FE Engage is my favorite Fire Emblem map, and probably the most fun I've ever had in the franchise. It accomplishes an absolute identity between story and gameplay by telling the former with the latter, and it is exactly that kind of experience that I wanted to be able to recreate at the table. What does traditional DnD-esque roleplaying become when we throw in a larger roster of player characters, permadeath that advances rather than dead-ends a story, and whole map structured encounters? Well, in my experience of privately running this system for over a year, what you get is a damn good time.

Campaign Design

Emblem RPG is best suited to a campaign with a story that involves a large party. It is built into the premises of this game system that your players will be leading a retinue of followers (their Retainers), and that there is no reason for your players' main characters (their Lord units) to ever really betray each other. Lyn, Eliwood and Hector are a good example case of this, or for instance, the various lords and retainers of FE: Fates. Emblem RPG is not really designed to be a system where PVP is intended, although, some implementation of this may be possible if there is enough interest.

I have run this game for play contexts involving 1 player, 2 players and 3 players. Beyond that, I cannot speak to the play experience of a larger table size in this system.

As a GM, you will want to begin building a campaign by establishing for each player at least one Retainer, and supply the narrative reasoning for why that Retainer has sufficient reason to follow the player character. It could be their family member, a dutiful attendant, a lifelong friend, a hired sword, etc, etc. For table sizes of 1 or 2 players, you may want to give them more Retainers, e.g. 4-5 retainers for a single player's starting retinue, and 2 or 3 retainers for a duo.

Making Lords

In order to keep the cohesion of the party for the sake of what this game system intends for its narrative experience, you ought to provide your players with structure when it comes to who their driver character, their Lord, may be. This doesn't necessarily mean you make their character for them, but it does mean that you need to have some idea of the *role* within the broader campaign narrative that you need that character to play. Again, you might ask yourself, "who's the Lyn" of this group, or "who's the Eliwood." You could alternative take a leaf out of Sacred Stones, if it were a duo campaign, and ask "who's the Ephraim? who's the Erika?", and so forth. Who's going to be the 'Alm' that commands the martial forces of the group? Who's going to be the 'Celica' who has more magical ties to the metaphysical conflicts happening in the realm?

The reason to do this is to establish character roles and motivations that will guide the future orientation of the party, and provide a strong foundation for story moving forward. You probably *should not* have the players be a rag-tag band of misfits with no prior relation to one another, with different motivations and interests, with no prior connection to the events of the plot, all suddenly caroused by fate to be in the same group, unless you and your players *really know what you're doing*.

Making Retainers

In the same vein as making Lords deliberately and with intention, the players' followers as well must be done with intention. Using FE as a conceptual guide here is going to be helpful. Which Lord is going to have your red and green cavaliers? Which Lord is going to have a Jagen? Which Lord is going to have the trainee unit that starts off weaker than the rest, but has higher growth rates? While these are all questions to be asked mechanically, it is equally important to consider, again, the narrative reason the retainer is following the Lord. Furthermore, unless your play group has experience with this system or are experienced TTRPG players in general, I would recommend making Retainers all pre-mades.

Structure of Play

Emblem RPG is designed to be structured around discrete play-sessions where the play group intentionally engages with cycles between a Map Encounter and Downtime. Think modern FE: the game sets you up with some story, then there's a map, and then you go into a 'hub world' for some downtime and more story, and then there's another map. Emblem RPG expects you do to exactly this. The game is NOT designed for players to be doing intermittent combat while doing exploration, as one might expect from more traditional TTRPGs like DnD or Pathfinder. Players will not be running into random monsters in the woods and having a one-shot combat encounter. Rather, the intention is for the GM and the Players to be doing combat as Map Encounters with deliberate design and intention behind it.

For the reason, it is important for the GM to conduct downtime play-sessions in such a way that *what* the next map needs to be becomes self-evident, and once committed, there's no backing down. In this way, the GM can avoid rail-roading players, while still preparing structured Map Encounters that deliver on what Emblem RPG is designed to do: let you play Fire Emblem, but in a TTRPG kind of environment.

Play Example (Read This!)

For example, I'll present a run down of the first couple sessions that I ran in my own campaign using this system:

Session 0: I present my group of 3 players with a dossier on what the campaign will be. I show them three 'roles' that already fit into the overall plot I have in mind, those being:

  • 'The Hero': I told them this is sort of the 'the Eliwood' of the group. He's going to be a powerful aristocrat getting into a major political marriage. The disaster that befalls that marriage sets off the whole campaign.

  • 'The Ally': I presented this role as 'the Hector' of the group. He's the Hero character's old time best friend, someone who has ties to other important factions involved in the central plot.

  • 'The Stranger': I presented this role as someone who is a bit of 'the Celica'; she has prophetic connections to the events and disasters that will befall the Hero's wedding, and has come to the wedding to try and prevent that calamity.

In Session 0, players talk amongst themselves about which role they wish to fill, and negotiate with the GM about how the GM is going to plan out these units mechanically. This is where players can have some voice about what kind of Class they want their Lord to be. The GM can say that the Hero and the Ally must be martials, while the Stranger must be a magical unit, but it's in session 0 that players can petition for specifics. The GM then designs for the Lord units a custom class, or they may approve of or work with a player in laying out a progression path for themselves. (see @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.lV3gzXJS8TZfYlli]{Making Custom Content})

Session 1: (Exposition) This was an all RP session with no combat. It's the lead-up to the Hero's wedding, and all we do is have the main characters talk. They meet each other, they roleplay, they roll skill checks, they talk to Retainers, so on and so on. It's important to rail-road *a little bit* here; the purpose of this session is not yet really to play the game. It's to establish exposition and for the characters to come alive a little bit, and for the players to start to emotionally invest in them. We need to establish:

  • Who these characters are

  • What is their investment in the happenings of the campaign's plot

  • Why we should care

The end of this session should lead directly into what the GM's first prepared combat map will be. For us, it was this attack at the Hero's wedding. The whole first session of this campaign was just to make it so that when this attack happens, it feels like it matters.

Session 2: (Map Encounter) This session picked up exactly where the previous one left off: the characters have been properly introduced, the wedding is under way, and we begin straight away with this attack. The battle map I used was one designed to be the scenery of this wedding ceremony itself. Units are placed on the board, roughly approximating where I think each character would be as this ambush is happening. I then present the various Objectives of the map:

  • Escape: The map succeeds when you get your Lords to these arrival points on the map, in which case they flee the scene of the wedding.

  • Defeat Boss: The map may also succeed if you manage to defeat the Big Bad who is at the heart of this attack. Its death means that the rest of the attack will end as well.

  • Survive: After X amount of turns, the city guard will arrive to rescue whoever is still alive.

I also present some classic FE side objectives:

  • A Recruitable NPC: They notice something special about one of attackers. I say that she may yet be convinced to switch sides, given a good enough Sociability skill check.

  • Chests: Can they reach and recover the Hero's wedding gifts before they're looted by the enemy?

These decisions interred within the map itself is what, I think, lets the map tell its own kind of story in the way that players choose how to approach it. This session takes up the whole of the combat, e.g., in players playing out the map, and ends right when they succeed or fail.

Session 3: (Downtime) Now we go back into a pure RP session. Characters digest what just happened. They talk, they advance the story, they convene with their Retainers for more RP, etc. I set them up with a respite area, e.g., a Party Camp, where their units can spend Downtime Actions (see @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.sYye0P93AGik9kMZ]) to actualize how they prepare for what comes next. They buy items from vendors, repair/forge equipment, build Support XP among units, train units, cook for boosts to growth rates, etc, etc.

Most importantly, out of all of this, this is where players as characters *make campaign decisions*. Since this is still a TTRPG and not a video game, what the next map encounter *is*, is not yet pre-determined. The players have to set up for the GM what to plan for next. That is the true goal of this session beyond simply doing mechanical prep and roleplaying the character drama. The GM has to know *what comes next* and what the players want to do. For instance, in our case, I presented the scenario before them as leading to three options. They all just survived this attack on the wedding in the capital city of the setting. They can either:

  • Flee back to the Hero's lands to raise their forces

  • Seize the city

  • Pursue those responsible by venturing North

These decisions can be communicated by the GM through the player Lord's conversations with their Retainers. However it comes about, and however the players choose their path, the GM needs to have adequate information so as to make the next Map Encounter all about actualizing that decision. In our case, my players chose the first option: flee and gather more allies, so I made the next map an Escape map.

Session 4: (Map Encounter). From the previous session, my players affirmed their decision to make their way back to the Hero's vassal-lands. So naturally, the map I prepared was 'what waylays them as they proceed along that path'. This was an Escape map: seeing as the attack at the wedding failed to kill one of its prime targets (the Hero), the assassins are in active pursuit. Before the players can make it back to safe territory, they must pass through one more bold attempt by the enemy.

Session 5: (Downtime Again). And from here you can kind of start to see the structure of how this all goes. Players make it safely to another hub, e.g. the fortress of an allied barony. They engage in hub world activities. They talk, they plan, they roleplay, they build up relationships more and more between themselves and the retainers, and so on. Through this session, the GM gets an affirmation from the players on what their plans are next, and uses that information to prepare the next map encounter.

Controls/Keybindings

To command a unit, you take it up, pick where it goes, then choose what it does, mostly from the keyboard. Every key below can be rebound under Configure Controls in Foundry's settings.

Default Key

What It Does

Select and Confirm

Space

Takes up the unit under your cursor, or confirms a move, a target or an open prompt.

Cancel and Put Down

Shift or Escape

Steps back one choice: drops targeting, undoes a move, or puts the unit down. Double-clicking empty ground does the same.

Cycle Units

Tab

Jumps to the nearest unit that still has a turn to take. If it’s yours, press Select and Confirm (Space) to take control of it.

F

Opens a door or chest, takes from a Loot pile, uses a downtime station, or mans a weapon on the ground.

Marks the friendly units beside this one. Click one to swap items with it.

Hotbar slots

1 to 0; Alt + 1 to 0; Ctrl + 1 to 0

Uses the item or ability in that slot of the first, second or third hotbar row.

Show Token Tooltip

Hold this and point at a token to read its stats.

While a token tooltip is open, shows the unit’s stats as if it held its next weapon.

Shows what each square of terrain does.

Q

Pulls the camera back to show the whole map.

You can also take up a unit by right-clicking it, and walk it with Foundry's movement keys or by dragging it along the highlighted squares. Since Space is now used to select and confirm, Foundry's pause key moves to P. Foundry's keys for raising and lowering token elevation are turned off as well, because a unit's elevation comes from the map's terrain data, which you set up in the Terrain Builder app.

Core Settings

You'll find these in Foundry's settings, under the Emblem RPG system.

World settings can only be changed by the GM:

  • Difficulty. Normal, Veteran, Extreme or Lunatic. Each step above Normal makes every Enemy and Boss unit stronger, while Lords, Retainers, Allies and Neutral units are left alone. The HP bonus is a percentage of the unit's final max HP, and the rest are flat bonuses:

  • Hit Chance Model. How attacks, skill checks and saving throws are rolled. The chances shown in the Combat Preview are the same under every model; what changes is how the dice actually behave.

    • Karmic (the default). Each side, players and enemies, keeps a hidden luck balance. When a side's rolls go worse than their odds, like missing two 80% attacks in a row, its next rolls are quietly re-rolled with the better result kept, up to three times. A run of good luck is evened out the same way. Over a session the odds hold up, without long streaks. Pick this if you want the shown chances to feel fair.

    • True RNG. A single d20, exactly as shown, with no correction. Streaks will happen. Pick this if your table wants pure, unforgiving dice.

    • Two Random Numbers. Each roll averages two d20s instead of rolling one, as in the classic Fire Emblem games. High chances become safer and low chances riskier than they look: a shown 70% actually hits about 85% of the time, and a shown 30% about 18%. Pick this if your table wants plans that hold up, with the occasional lucky dodge.

  • Flyer Targeting. Aerial (the default) stops melee weapons from targeting flying units. Classic lets melee hit an adjacent flier within the normal height limit.

  • XP Multiplier. Scales all XP earned. 1 is normal and 0 awards none (see @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.EKqsPYVWwd9HQqoq#experience]{Experience}).

  • To Player Crit Dmg. Multiplier. Scales down the extra damage enemy critical hits deal to Lords and Retainers. At 0.5, 10 extra damage becomes 5.

  • Token Outline Colour. The exact colour of the outline drawn around every token's art, #382040 by default. This setting doesn't draw an outline itself; it tells the system which colour to look for. Each scene's configuration has a Token Outline Color field, beside its background colour, and on that scene every pixel of token art in the outline colour is recoloured to the scene's choice. That way, outlines can stand out against a light or a dark map. For this to work, all of your token art has to draw its outline in this one colour, matched almost exactly: art outlined in any other shade is left unchanged. If your token art uses a different outline colour, set this to match it.

  • Lock Token Artwork Rotation. Locks down a token's rotation. It's on by default, so that Emblem RPG's GBA-style sprite art stays side-facing and tokens don't get rotated by accident with the mouse wheel.

Client settings are set by each player for themselves:

  • Camera: Battle, Abilities, Casting and Item Usage. Whether the camera zooms in, with letterboxing, when each kind of action happens. Camera: Zoom sets how close it gets.

  • Camera: Phase Opening. As a phase opens, the camera pans to each unit taking damage from a status or hazard, then to your party.

  • Camera: Enemy Phase Zoom. How far the camera pulls back during the Enemy Phase.

  • Camera: Center on Selection and Centering Speed. Whether, and how quickly, the camera pans to a unit you take up.

  • Camera: Follow Movement, Follow Margin and Follow Speed. How the camera tracks a moving unit: not at all, panning when the unit nears the edge of the screen, or keeping it centred.

  • Terrain Tips. Whether the Show Terrain Tips key shows tips while held, or toggles them on and off.

  • Token Tooltip Scale. The size of the tooltip you get when holding the Show Token Tooltip key (Alt by default) and hovering your mouse over a token.

  • Voiceline Frequency. How often units speak when selected: Normal, Extended (30 seconds between lines), Once Per Phase, or Disabled.

  • UI Sounds. All, Game Only (mutes the sounds on sheets and menus), or None.

Character Creation

Emblem RPG is pretty freeform when it comes to how you want to design a Lord or player character unit. To make player characters feel special, you ought to design a custom class for them. This can be as simple as taking an existing base class, giving it a different name, and tweaking its offered stats, proficiencies and features.

As a Rule of Thumb for balancing a custom class, simply take what is offered by a different class at an equivalent level, and swap things around. For instance, suppose you wanted to make a Lord unit who was special by virtue of being able to wield both sword and sorcery. You could combine the Initiate and Trainee starter classes by simply swapping out the Features a Trainee gets at Level 1 (Precaution/Swap or Deflection) with the choice of spells an Initiate has at Level 1. Then you could split the D rank in Blade weapons the Trainee has into E rank in Blade and E rank in Elemental magic. Then you might take 1 point off of the Trainee's Agi and Tqn, and put those 2 points into the unit's Wit to support their spellcasting. The result would be a hybrid class, unique to a player character's Lord, that is nevertheless mostly balanced with the rest of the system.

Player Driven Character Creation

If You Want To Give Players Freedom in designing their own custom class in this way, you can let them create this themselves by following these recommended guidelines (Players must have Trusted Player permissions before being able to edit their Class document):

  • 1) Players first pick a baseline class to start with, e.g. Trainee or Initiate.

  • 2) Players may modify the Proficiencies of the class, by subtracting a rank in a Proficiency and granting it to a different Proficiency.

    • Players may gain another Proficiency rank to distribute however they please, but if they choose to do so, they must forgo the Stat Bonus Allocation step in 4).

  • 3) Players may modify the Skills of the class, by picking any combination of Skills as long as they accord with one of the following distributions:

    • d4, d4, d6

    • d6, d6

    • If the unit's baseline class was Thief, then they may reassign their Skill allocation as what the Thief had: d4, d4, d6, d6

  • 4) Players may modify the Core Stats of the Class (Mgt, Agi, Tqn, Wit, Cha, Def or Res) as follows:

    • Stat Bonus: Allocate +1 to two stats of your choosing. They must be different stats.

    • Stat Shifting: Subtract 1 point from another Core Stat to allocate it to another Core Stat.

    • Fixed Stats: The base class's HP, Stn, Eva, Bld, Spd and Acc cannot be modified this way. These remain the same as what is granted by the chosen base class.

  • 5) Players may establish their Growth Rates as follows:

    • For Lord Units: they have 30 points to distribute however they please on top of the base class's growth rates.

    • For Retainer Units: they have 20 points.

    • This distribution should NOT be done on the Class document sheet, but rather as a direct modifier on the Character sheet itself (right clicking the stat whose growth you want to distribute into). Otherwise, upon a Class change via Promotion, the unit's allocated Growth Rates will disappear.

    • Power Scaling: Depending on how powerful you want your players to be, you may bump up the Growth Rate distribution you assign to players. I do not recommend giving them more than 45 points. Emblem RPG is a low-number system and is balanced around each stat gain being more impactful than in traditional Fire Emblem.

  • 6) Players adjust their Stat Limits by taking the Limits granted by the chosen base class, and modifying them based on how they approached step 4. For example, if in step 4, I allocated 2 points to Mgt, but subtracted 1 point from Wit, then in my Stat limits, I increase the Mgt limit by 2, and decrease the limit for Wit by 1.

  • 7) Each starting class (besides Bard) grants Features at level 1, 3 and 5. Players may choose 1 of those Feature bundles to swap out for the Feature bundle of another starter class of the same Level. For example, suppose a player's chosen base class is Hunter. They might elect to swap out the Lv 3 Feature 'Into the Wilds' for the Lv 3 Feature bundle of Acolyte 'Shine or Restore'. Players ought to make sure that the abilities they're swapping for can actually be used by them (e.g. in this case, the player needs to have made sure that their unit can actually cast Divine magic in Step 2).

    • An ability marked 'Unique' may NOT be acquired this way, as they are only accessible to the base class that has starts with it.

  • 8) Finally, rename the Class to fit the theme of what has been created. E.g. following step 7, we might call this a 'Demon Hunter' unique Class.

  • 9) The GM always has final approval authority over what custom class a Player wants to devise.

  • 10) ADVANCED: To plan out a unit's full Class trajectory, we must also grapple with the unit's future Promotion classes. I will save this for a future guide, as the above should suffice for now for getting players started on a new campaign.

GM Pre-Made Character Classes

If you want players to follow premade custom classes you plot out for their Characters (this is what I do), then you as the GM have free reign to do whatever you please in setting up unique Lord units starting class and unique promotion classes. However, I would advise still giving players some freedom in building their character by allowing them:

  • The same freedom to allocate their character specific Growth Rates (30-45 for Lords, 20-30 for Retainers).

  • The same freedom to assign their Skills' dice distribution.

  • Choices to be made at certain Level Thresholds in terms of what Features they want to adopt. The game's shipped premade Classes already have several examples of this. Letting players choose what Features they want to obtain at specific Lv thresholds, and letting them choose what they want to Promote into (the options are still predetermined by you here), will make it so that players do not have freedom in how their character starts out, but they will have a great deal of freedom over the final build the character has throughout their progression. This is the more intended way to play Emblem RPG.

Starting Equipment

Each player starts with 1000 GP to spend on their starter equipment and items, and an additional 500 GP for each Retainer that they have. Players must ensure that each unit has a piece of Armor equipped, and if they are a martial unit, one weapon. Other than that, players have freedom to purchase any Equipment or Consumable item within the game's directory that they have sufficient funding for.

Personal Abilities

The GM is encouraged to set up each Lord and Retainer with a Personal passive ability (similar to a lot of modern FE). This can be as simple as making a flat EXP bonus multiplier, a custom passive aura for a Retainer that grants their Lord +3 Atk while standing next to that Lord, or something like Bernadetta's ability to get bonus to Atk while injured. See (@UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.lV3gzXJS8TZfYlli]{Making Custom Content} for more details).


Setting Up A Party

In Emblem RPG, a Party is a group of players and their owned units. Each player belongs to at most one party, and each unit belongs to the party of whichever player owns it. Usually, that means each player owns their Lord and the Retainers who follow them, the same retinue you lay out in @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.CgEUqW0uzVMKrBdY#campaign-design]{Campaign Design}. Which party a unit is in matters for:

  • Downtime. Units only cook for, perform with, socialize with and train members of their own party. A unit in no party works alone (see the @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.sYye0P93AGik9kMZ]{Downtime page}).

  • Rally. A unit can Rally any member of its party, at the None tier if they share no Support rank yet. A unit outside the party needs a Support rank first (see @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.EKqsPYVWwd9HQqoq#support]{Support}).

  • Shared sight. The Lords, Retainers and Allies of one party share their vision. An Ally in no party shares its vision with every party.

  • Vendors. Haggles and buybacks are tracked for each party.

  • The Convoy. Each party can have one, covered below.

The party doesn't decide sides or phases in combat, or who earns XP. Those follow each unit's faction (see @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.fRmf6UOHviDS5kFI#unit-factions]{Unit Factions}). Trading also works between any friendly units, party or not.

The Configure Party Menu

You'll find Configure Party at the top of the Actors directory. Only the Gamemaster can make changes in it; an Assistant GM sees the button, but can't save anything. Every actor and Convoy needs to be in the world, not sitting in a compendium. To set up a party:

  1. Create each player's Lord and Retainers as Character actors, and a Convoy actor for the party.

  2. Press Create Party in the window's header and give the party a name.

  3. Tick the party's players, and drop the Convoy into its Convoy field.

  4. In each player's card, drop in their Lord and Retainers.

Parties pane.

  • Rename (pen) and Delete (bin). Deleting a party unassigns its players and ends their access to its Convoy, but it doesn't change who owns which unit.

  • Convoy. Drop a Convoy actor here to link it. The × unlinks it.

  • Players. Tick each player in the party. Ticking a player moves them out of any other party.

Players pane. There's one card per player, which you can collapse or expand by clicking its header.

  • Lord. Drop the player's Lord here. The player becomes its owner, its faction is set to Lord (after a confirmation, if it was another type), and it becomes the player's Player Character in Foundry's user configuration.

  • Retainers. Drop the player's Retainers here. The player becomes the owner of each one, and its faction is set to Retainer. The list shows every other Character the player owns.

  • Drag between cards to hand a unit over to another player; the first player loses ownership of it. Drag between Lord and Retainers on the same card to change its role.

  • × removes the player's ownership of a unit. Its faction stays as it was.

  • UUID gives the player ownership of an actor or a placed token by its UUID, such as an unlinked token on a scene, without changing its faction.

Party-mates automatically get Observer on each other's units, so they can read each other's sheets, and on their party's Convoy. These are taken away again once the players no longer share a party.

Party Convoys

Just like in Fire Emblem, the Convoy is the party's shared storage, here for both items and gold. It lives on a Convoy actor. Once you link it in Configure Party, every unit the party's players own uses it as its linked Convoy. The Convoy doesn't need to be placed on the map.

The Convoy sheet. It holds Equipment, Consumables, Miscellaneous items and Resources, sorted into tabs, along with a GP total. Stored and Inbound switch between what's in the Convoy and what's on its way.

  • Stored. As the GM, you can drop items in, delete them and edit the GP.

  • Inbound. Goods and gold on their way, which players can see but can't take yet. Requisitioned gold arrives here, and you can drop in items to deliver later. Deliver moves everything into the Convoy. Right-click an item to deliver it alone, or the coin for Deliver gold.

What a linked Convoy does.

  • Vendors. With Send to Convoy ticked, purchases go straight to the Convoy and are paid from the unit's purse first, then the Convoy's gold. A unit can also sell off the Convoy's stock, and the proceeds go to the Convoy.

  • Gathering. The haul goes to the Convoy by default, or to the unit.

  • Forging, Alchemy and Cooking. The item to forge can be kept in the Convoy, and materials and ingredients are drawn from the unit's pockets first, then the Convoy. Crafted Potions and Bombs go to the Convoy when the unit's pockets are full.

  • Equipment slots. Equipment beyond a unit's slots is sent to the Convoy.

  • Requisitioning. This needs a linked Convoy. Granted gold arrives as inbound gold.

Player access. Players open the Convoy with the house button (Open Linked Convoy) at the top of the inventory on a unit's character sheet. The Convoy sheet is read-only for players, and items are moved by dragging:

  • Take an item: drag it from the Convoy onto the unit's sheet.

  • Take gold: drag the coin onto the unit's sheet and choose an amount.

  • Store an item: drag it onto the Convoy's Stored view, or press the item's Drop Item button and choose Move to Convoy.

Outside an encounter, the Convoy can be used from anywhere. During an encounter, players can't take anything out of it, but a unit can still store items while it has some of its turn left, at no action cost. As the GM, you can take from a Convoy at any time.

User Permissions

Emblem RPG handles permissions a little differently from most Foundry systems. Commanding a unit and editing it are kept separate: players command their units through the system, while only the GM and Trusted Players edit documents.

The GM's Client

Every game action, whether that's moving, attacking, using an item, trading or a Downtime activity, is sent to the GM's client, which checks it and writes the result. Players never write these changes themselves. For this to work, exactly one Gamemaster needs to be connected, with the world open in one browser tab:

  • With no Gamemaster connected, players can't act. An Assistant GM can't stand in.

  • With two Gamemasters connected, or the world open in two of the GM's tabs, play stops until only one is left.

  • While the GM's client carries out an action, input on every client waits until it's done.

  • While the game is paused, Players and Trusted Players can't act. GMs and Assistant GMs can.

Roles

Player. In plain Foundry, owning an actor lets a player edit it however they like. In Emblem RPG, ownership only lets them play it.

  • The unit's sheet opens read-only. Its gameplay controls still work: equipping and wielding, mounting, dropping items, skill rolls, choosing class features, moving items between the player's own units, and the Convoy.

  • The player can't rename the unit, change its stats, skills, proficiencies, XP, Supports or class, open its Control Panel, or drag in items from the directory or a compendium.

  • The player can't select or drag tokens freely. A unit is taken up through the system, moves only along its highlighted squares, and only during an encounter or Free Exploration. Box selection and Foundry's Token HUD are turned off.

  • These limits apply to Foundry's interface. They won't stop a player who edits documents from the browser console.

Trusted Player. Can also edit the units, items and classes they own. This is the role to give a player who builds their own custom class.

  • Their sheets become editable, including the right-click editors and the Control Panel (unit type, faction, voice path and token art). A voice-line folder still needs a GM's approval.

  • They can assign classes and Support partners.

  • Outside an encounter, they can select and drag their own tokens as in plain Foundry.

  • They still can't use the Token HUD or box selection, change ownership, edit item descriptions or images, or use GM tools.

  • Emblem RPG Studio stays closed to them until you tick them under Trusted Player Studio Access in the module's settings.

GM and Assistant GM. Both can edit any document, run encounters, use the Terrain Builder, handle tokens freely and act while the game is paused. Only the Gamemaster's client runs game actions, though, and only the Gamemaster can save changes in Configure Party.

Observer

  • A Character or Object sheet only opens for users with Observer or higher.

  • Observer grants no vision. In plain Foundry, Observer lets a player see through a token; here, a token only gives sight to its owners and their party.

  • That means you can give players Observer on enemies, so they can read their stats and sheets while planning their moves, without seeing through their eyes. The content module's enemies already ship with Observer for all players.

The Control Lock

Only one unit can be commanded at a time across the whole table. While someone has a unit taken up, no one else, the GM included, can take up any unit, and everyone else is told who is selecting. The lock is released when the unit is put down or finishes acting. If the person holding it disconnects, the unit goes back to where its move began and the lock is freed. A unit owned by several players can be commanded by any of them, one at a time.

If the table ever gets stuck, a GM or Assistant GM can type one of these in chat:

  • /release frees the control lock, even from a player who is still connected.

  • /unstuck clears an action stuck in progress. The control lock stays until /release.

Stats

A unit's stats live in two places on its character sheet. The Stats column down the left side holds its core stats, and the row of numbers under the inventory holds its derived combat stats.

Core Stats

Core stats come from the unit's class, the gains it's made on level-up, and its gear and effects. A red number in brackets next to a stat is a penalty currently lowering it.

  • HP (Hit Points). How much damage the unit can take before it falls. Every point of Mgt adds 1 max HP.

  • Stn (Stance). The unit's battle posture. Break (Brk) damage wears it down, and at 0 the unit is Stance Broken: it can't use its Action or counterattack, takes -4 to Mgt, Agi, Tqn, Wit and Cha, and loses the Def, Res and Eva its armor and shield give. Worn armor and shields raise max Stn.

  • Mov (Movement). How many squares the unit can move on its phase.

  • Bld (Build). How much equipment Weight the unit can carry before it slows down. Every 4 points of Mgt add 1 Bld, and each point of Wgt over Bld costs 1 Agi.

  • Mgt (Might). Physical strength. Adds to Atk with weapons that scale on Might, adds 1 max HP per point, and adds 1 Bld for every 4 points.

  • Agi (Agility). Quickness. Each point adds 1 Spd, and every 2 points add 1 Eva.

  • Tqn (Technique). Precision. Each point adds 1 Acc and makes critical hits deal 5% more damage.

  • Wit. Cunning and intellect. Adds to Atk with weapons and spells that scale on Wit, and each point adds 1% to total Crit chance.

  • Cha (Charisma). Presence and fortune. Each point lowers an enemy's chance to land a critical hit on this unit by 1%. A higher Cha also widens the unit's Rally range.

  • Def (Defense). Subtracted from every hit of physical damage: Slashing, Piercing, Crushing, Missile, and untyped damage like an unarmed attack. So a 12 damage hit against 10 Def deals 2.

  • Res (Resistance). Subtracted from every hit of magical damage: Fire, Ice, Lightning, Wind, Arcane, Decay, Shadow and Holy.

Derived Stats

The combat stats row is worked out from the core stats and the unit's equipped weapon or spell, armor and shield, so these numbers shift whenever its stats, gear, terrain or effects do.

  • Wgt (Weight). The total Weight of the equipped weapon or spell, armor and shield. It turns red on the sheet when it's over Bld, and each point over is taken off the unit's Agi.

  • Rng (Range). How many squares away the equipped weapon or spell can reach, like 1 or 1-2. A unit can only counterattack an attacker within its Rng.

  • Eva (Evasion). The armor's Eva plus half of Agi (rounded down), plus any terrain bonus. Each point lowers an attacker's chance to hit by 5%.

  • Acc (Accuracy). The weapon's Acc plus Tqn. To hit, the attacker rolls d20 + Acc and has to beat the target's Eva, so each point adds 5% to hit. For example, 6 Acc against 12 Eva hits on a 7 or higher (70%).

  • Spd (Speed). Equal to Agi, plus any bonuses. As in Fire Emblem, being faster than your opponent lets you strike more than once: 4 Spd faster earns 1 extra attack in an exchange, and 8 faster earns 2.

  • Crit (Critical). The weapon's Crit plus Wit. The chance to land a critical hit is Crit minus the target's Cha and its armor's Crit Reduction, as a percentage. For example, 11 Crit against 4 Cha is a 7% chance. A critical hit deals double damage, plus 5% for each point of Tqn.

  • Atk (Attack). Damage per hit: the weapon or spell's Atk plus its scaling stat. Most weapons scale on Mgt and spells on Wit; some scale on Tqn, and Hybrid weapons use Mgt up close and Wit at range. The target's Def or Res is subtracted on a hit.

Hidden Stats

A few stats never show up on the character sheet. Gear, statuses and features can still change them, and you can use them as modifier targets in your own custom items.

  • Brk (Break). How much Stn damage the unit's hits deal, set by its weapon or spell.

  • Brk Red. (Break Reduction). Lowers the Brk damage the unit takes. Very few things grant this stat for now.

  • Crit Dmg (Crit Damage). The critical hit multiplier: x2, plus 0.05 for each point of Tqn. So 10 Tqn makes a unit's crits deal x2.5 damage.

  • Crit Red. (Crit Reduction). Lowers an attacker's chance to land a critical hit on the unit.

  • Weight Red. (Weight Reduction). Subtracted from the unit's total Wgt.

  • Stn Regen (Stance Regen). How much Stn the unit gets back if it ends its turn without taking any action. 3 by default. A Stance Broken unit that rests gets all of its Stn back.

  • Sight. Extra squares of vision on top of the unit's normal sight.

  • XP % (XP Multiplier). Scales the experience the unit earns. 100% is normal.

Stat Limits

Each class sets a limit on HP, Mgt, Agi, Tqn, Wit, Cha, Def and Res. The limit only counts the class base plus the gains the unit has earned. Bonuses from gear, statuses and other modifiers don't count toward it, so they can still push the total past it.

  • Reaching the limit. Once a stat's class base plus its gains reaches the limit, its number on the sheet turns turquoise. That stat stops growing on level-up, and the level-up screen marks it as capped.

  • Stat boosters stop at the limit too. A booster that would go over only raises the stat as far as the limit.

  • Raising the limit. Promoting to a new class swaps in that class's limits and keeps every gain the unit has made. Item and feature modifiers can also raise a limit.

  • No limit. A stat the class sets no limit for has none, and neither does any stat on a class with the Unplayable tier. Stn, Mov and Bld never have a limit.

A class's limits are listed on its class sheet. As the GM, you can still type a stat's Value past its limit by hand.

Special Stats

On the 'Features' tab of the character sheet, you will see the following stats: Extra Lives, Extra Actions, Dexterity and Willpower. These are meant for exceptionally powerful units, e.g. Bosses, or any other story NPC the GM may have in mind. These are akin to 'Legendary Actions' or 'Legendary Resistances' in DnD5e, if you are familiar. There may be rare cases when you grant these to a player unit for a variety of narrative reasons as well. Here's what they do:

  • Extra Lives. A hit that would defeat the unit spends one instead, and the unit comes back on the spot at full HP and full Stance. Each remaining life is shown as a heart on the token. Extra Lives never refill on their own; you give them back by hand on the sheet.

  • Extra Actions. After the unit attacks or uses an item during an encounter, it's asked whether to use an Extra Action. Taking one gives it its Standard Action, Bonus Action and full movement back, so it can move and act again. Only one can be used per turn, and the pool only refills when an encounter begins. E.g. a Boss with 2 Extra Actions can take up to three full turns a round for the first two rounds it chooses to.

  • Dexterity. Dexterity imposes Disadvantage on all attacks made against the unit, for the first # of attacks made against it per round equal to its Dexterity stat. An attacker with Advantage, from a Mark or the weapon triangle for instance, cancels out this Disadvantage and is brought back to a plain roll.

  • Willpower. Whenever the unit has to make a saving throw against a spell, ability or bomb, it spends one charge to roll the save with Advantage. This happens on its own, with no prompt. Each Willpower point is recovered at the start of every phase, just as Dexterity.

On the sheet, click a heart to turn an Extra Life on or off, and use the + and - beside it to set the maximum, up to 3. The other three show remaining over maximum: type the remaining number in the box, and use + and - to set the maximum.

Skills

Skills cover everything a unit can do outside of fighting. Each skill has a rank from untrained up to 4, shown on the sheet as a die: d4, d6, d8 or d10. Skills improve the more they're used.

A skill check rolls d20, plus the skill's die, plus a bonus from the skill's linked stat: +1 at 4, +2 at 7, +3 at 10, +4 at 15, +5 at 20 and +6 at 26 or higher. The total has to beat the DC to succeed. Click a skill's icon on the sheet to roll it normally, with Advantage, or with Disadvantage. You can call for a check whenever the moment calls for it, and the system calls for them itself during Downtime actions, stealing, lockpicking and some terrain crossings.

  • Athletics (Mgt). Strength and physical exertion: climbing, jumping, swimming and lifting. Used for most Gathering, and for climbing between elevations on the map.

  • Finesse (Agi). Agility, balance and sleight of hand. Used for Stealing and for some elevation crossings.

  • Trading (Cha). Commerce, bargaining and appraisal. Used for Haggling.

  • Civics (Wit). Knowledge of politics, history and social lore. Used for Requisitioning.

  • Handicraft (Tqn). Craftsmanship and mechanical skill. Used for Forging and for opening locks.

  • Sociability (Cha). Persuasion, charm and conversation. Used for Socializing.

  • Command (Cha). Leadership and intimidation: the force of a commanding presence. Used for Training.

  • Nature (Tqn). Knowledge of the wild: plants, animals, survival and herbal lore. Used for Cooking and Alchemy.

  • Perception (Tqn). Awareness: noticing hidden details, danger and deception.

  • Performance (Cha). Music, dance and showmanship. Used for Performing.

  • Reason (Wit). Academic knowledge and scholarly magic.

  • Esoteric (Cha). Knowledge of and attunement with spiritual practice, such as ritual and prayer-based magic.

Proficiencies

Proficiencies are a unit's weapon ranks, covering both weapons and magic, from E up to S. A unit can only wield an item if it holds the rank the item asks for.

  • Brawling. Gauntlets and claws that hit weakly but often, since most grant an Extra Attack.

  • Blade. Swift, accurate weapons with the widest range of options.

  • Polearm. Spears and lances with steady Piercing damage.

  • Heavy. Axes and hammers: the hardest hitters and the best at breaking Stance, but they often weigh you down and are inaccurate.

  • Bow. Ranged weapons that are deadly against Flying units but can't strike adjacent foes.

  • Covert. Daggers and throwing knives that weaken a target's stats with each hit.

  • Elemental. Fire, ice, wind and lightning: straightforward offensive magic, strong at breaking Stance.

  • Divine. Mostly healing and support spells, with some powerful radiant attacks at higher ranks.

  • Occult. Dark magic of curses, life drain and summoning.

  • Arcane. Mostly utility magic: teleportation, illusions and spells that lock enemies down.

  • Armor. The heaviest armor the unit can wear: Light, Medium or Heavy.

  • Riding. Whether the unit's class rides a horse or a flying mount.

Support

Supports are the bonds between Lords and Retainers, graded from E to S rank. Both units share a bond at the same rank, and it's shown on both of their character sheets.

Two units earn Support XP together when one Rallies the other for the first time in a map, and when they share a Downtime activity, like Cooking, Performing, Socializing or Training. You can also award Support XP yourself for good roleplay (see @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.U8ZRPd1EK3DZm5B0#awarding-character-interactions]{Awarding Character Interactions}). A new bond needs 50 XP to reach E, then 50 to D, 50 to C, 75 to B, 100 to A and 125 to reach S.

Affinities. Every Lord and Retainer has an Affinity, chosen on the Supports tab. An Affinity sets the stats the unit's Rally changes; most raise two stats and lower one. The tab shows which stats the chosen Affinity raises and lowers.

Rally. Every Lord and Retainer has the Rally ability, named after its Affinity (Rally: Caution, for example). Rally costs a Standard Action and affects up to 6 friendly units in range. Its range grows with the caster's Cha, from 1 square up to 5 squares at 14 Cha. Each target gains the caster's Affinity stats until the start of the target's next phase. The bond between caster and target decides how strong the Rally is:

  • A higher Support rank gives larger bonuses and smaller penalties.

  • A party member with no bond gets the weakest version. A unit outside the caster's party can only be Rallied if the two share a bond.

  • A caster can Rally the same unit once per map, twice at C rank, and three times at S rank. A unit can only receive one Rally per round.

Homebrewing Affinities

Each world keeps its own Affinity table in Data/worlds/<world>/json/affinities.json. The system copies the default table there the first time the world loads. You can edit this file to change the existing Affinities or add your own; every client then needs to reload for the changes to take effect. If the file can't be read, the system shows a warning and falls back to the default table. Deleting the file restores the defaults on the next load.

"Caution": {
  "label": "Caution",
  "adjective": "cautious",
  "stats": {
    "eva": { "None": 2, "E": 3, "D": 3, "C": 4, "B": 4, "A": 4, "S": 5 },
    "def": { "None": 2, "E": 3, "D": 3, "C": 3, "B": 4, "A": 5, "S": 5 },
    "atk": { "None": -4, "E": -4, "D": -3, "C": -3, "B": -3, "A": -2, "S": -1 }
  }
}

Each entry under affinities is one Affinity. label is the name players see, and adjective appears in the Rally's description. Under stats, each stat key (such as atk, eva or stnMax) lists its value at each tier: None for a Rally without a bond, then each Support rank. Negative values are penalties, and a tier you leave out counts as 0. The optional statLabels section sets how each stat's name is shown in-game.

Growth Rates

Each level-up rolls once for each of HP, Mgt, Agi, Tqn, Wit, Cha, Def and Res, just like Fire Emblem's growth rates. A stat's growth rate is its percent chance to rise by 1 on that roll, and a stat already at its limit won't rise. Press Show Growths on the sheet to see a unit's growth rates.

A unit's base growth rates come from its class, and they're only meant as a baseline. A unit raises them further through:

  • Cooking. Meals made through Cooking in Downtime can grant growth rate bonuses.

  • Boosters. Consumables like the Tinctures permanently raise one growth rate each.

  • Character creation. Players assign extra growth rates from a pool of points when making a character (see @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.t03al1QkHOCBns0f#character-creation]{Character Creation} under @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.t03al1QkHOCBns0f]{Getting Started}).

Budding Talent. A level-up where no stat rises, or only HP does, gives the unit Budding Talent: +10 to every growth rate on its next level-up. It goes away after a level-up that raises any stat other than HP.

Proficiency XP

Weapon and magic proficiencies earn XP as the unit uses them. Armor and Riding don't earn XP.

Each strike with a weapon or spell earns XP in its proficiency: 2 for a hit and 1 for a miss. Using items like staves can earn it too, and so can Downtime Training. The bar under each icon shows progress to the next rank. By default it takes 50 XP to reach E, then 50 for D, 75 for C, 100 for B and 125 for A.

A rank-up empties the bar, and XP beyond the threshold is lost. XP can raise a proficiency as far as A, but never to S.

Skill XP

Each skill has a rank from none up to 4, shown as its die: d4, d6, d8, then d10. Every skill roll earns 1 XP in that skill, whether it succeeds or fails, and Downtime actions earn skill XP as well.

Rank 1 takes 40 XP, then 60 for rank 2, 80 for rank 3 and 100 for rank 4. Leftover XP carries toward the next rank. At rank 4 the skill is mastered and earns no more XP.

Promotions

A class can have one or more promotion paths, each leading to a stronger class. A unit promotes by using a Promotion item from its inventory. The promotion window then lists every path the unit's class offers, and for the path you pick, it shows the new class's stats, limits, proficiencies and mount next to the current ones.

To take a path, the unit needs:

  • The right item. Each path names the Promotion item that unlocks it.

  • A minimum level, plus any proficiency and skill ranks the path asks for.

  • Its turn. During an encounter, the unit can't have finished its turn yet, and promoting ends it.

Paths the unit can't take yet stay in the list, showing what's missing.

When a unit promotes:

  • Its Class is replaced. The Class base stats, Class growth rates and stat limits all become the new class's. A stat can go down if the new class has a lower base, so check the window before you confirm.

  • What it's earned stays. Level, XP, stat gains, its own growth rates and its earned proficiency and skill ranks all carry over.

  • Proficiencies are recalculated. Weapon ranks become the unit's earned ranks plus the new class's grant. Armor becomes whatever the new class allows.

  • Features and mount change. The old Class's features are replaced by the new Class's, and a class that comes with a mount grants it. Any feature flagged as 'Unique' on the previous Class is lost, unless the new Class was declared as an exception.

  • The Promotion item is spent. One use comes off, or the item is removed if that was its last use.

As the GM, you can also promote a unit with the 'Promote Unit' macro in the 'Emblem RPG | Macros' compendium, which skips every requirement.

Other Forms of Progression

In Emblem RPG, units are meant to grow through their equipment and items just as much as through their levels:

  • Refining equipment. Forging in Downtime repairs weapons and armor, and every repair counts toward refining them tier by tier, so a favorite weapon can grow alongside its wielder.

  • Magical items and accessories. Found, bought or earned items can grant stat bonuses, features and abilities of their own.

  • Stat boosters. Consumables that permanently raise a stat, up to its limit.

  • Growth boosters. Consumables that permanently raise a growth rate, so every later level-up is more likely to pay off.

Voice-Overs

Any unit can be given its own voice lines. As the GM, you set them up per unit by pointing it at a folder of audio files.

  2. Inside it, create the subfolders below for the lines the unit should have, and put the audio files in them. Files can be .ogg, .wav or .mp3, and each time a line plays, one file is picked at random from its subfolder. Subfolder names have to match exactly, and a missing or empty subfolder is simply silent.

  3. Click the unit's portrait on its character sheet to open the Actor Control Panel, and enter the folder in Voice Path (or pick it with the folder button).
