Obtaining Voice-Over Files. I personally use voice over sound files found online from various gacha games' wiki pages, or ripped from other games in general. If you cannot access a direct download to a sound file, but the website allows you to hear it via a button press, you can use your browser console to access the file. Feel free to ask in the Discord server for advice about how to do this.

Setting Up A Combat

Unit Factions

Every unit belongs to one faction, which decides its side and when it acts:

  • Lord. A player's main character. Acts in the Player Phase.

  • Retainer. A unit in a player's retinue. Acts in the Player Phase.

  • Ally. A unit that fights for the players but belongs to no player. Acts in the Player Phase.

  • Enemy. An opposing unit. Acts in the Enemy Phase.

  • Boss. An opposing leader. Acts in the Enemy Phase, and defeating one is worth double XP.

  • Neutral. Hostile to both sides, but takes no phase of its own.

Lords, Retainers and Allies are friendly to each other, and so are Enemies and Bosses. Only Lords and Retainers earn XP and form Supports.

Placing Units

Every unit on the map is a Character actor. Drag the actors onto the scene, then open each one's Actor Control Panel (the Control Panel button in the character sheet header) and set its faction under Actor Type. The same panel sets the faction's name, icon and colour, and the unit's owners. Lord and Retainer tokens are always linked to their actors.

You can play enemies yourself, or hand them to the Enemy AI module, which adds a Combat AI tab to the Actor Control Panel (see @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.4bL4mJsYfkVkFUxV]{Configuring Enemy AI}). Hidden tokens don't count when the tracker checks whether a phase is finished, and you can set reinforcements to appear on terrain squares partway through the map (see @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.ZxXYJlf5ACElkTNj]{Using the Terrain Builder}).

Placing Drops or Loot

Drops. On an item carried by any unit other than a Lord or Retainer, the item sheet shows a Flag control. Set it to Drops and enter a percentage chance (blank means 100%). When the unit is defeated, each unequipped item flagged Drops rolls its chance, and the ones that pass fall in a Loot pile on its square.

Stealables. Set the Flag to Stealable and enter a DC. A unit with the Steal ability can steal from an adjacent enemy on the same level: it picks unequipped stealable items and makes one Finesse check against their combined DC. Success takes them all, and either way, the thief's turn ends. The combat tracker marks units carrying drops or stealable items with a sack icon.

Loot piles. A Loot pile is an Object actor whose contents any unit standing on it can take with the Interact key (default F). Defeated units leave them behind automatically, and you can also place one by hand.

Chests. Create an Object actor, set its type to Chest, and drag items into its Contents. A chest can be locked:

  • Key. Drag an item into the key slot. A unit carrying that item opens the chest outright and uses up the key.

  • DC. A unit with Locktouch can pick the lock with a Handicraft check against the DC. A DC of 0 makes the lock key-only.

Opening a lock during an encounter takes the unit's Standard Action and ends its turn. During Free Exploration, picking a lock costs 1 Energy instead (see @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.sYye0P93AGik9kMZ#chests/locks]{Chests/Locks}).

Setting Objectives

Objectives are saved on the scene. Set them with Set Objectives in the combat tracker, or from the Objectives card in the Terrain Builder. The dialog has two parts:

  • Defeat Conditions. Any Lord defeated ends the map in failure if a Lord falls. Protected Unit(s) lists other units whose defeat ends the map in failure. Round Limit ends the map in failure once that round closes (0 means no limit).

  • Win conditions. Each objective card picks one, and meeting any card wins the map:

    • Defeat Target(s): every named unit has to fall.

    • Rout Enemy: defeat a set number of enemies, or all of them if left blank.

    • Survive: hold out for the given number of rounds.

    • Arrive: the required units, or any one player unit, reach an Arrival Point. Units that arrive leave the map.

    • Defend: hold out for the given number of rounds. The map is lost if an enemy stands on a Defense Point.

Units can be named by token ID, actor ID or name. Arrival and Defense Points are painted onto squares in the Terrain Builder. While a Survive or Defend objective is set, the Round Limit isn't used. A won map shows Map Cleared!, and a lost one shows Defeat.

The Phase Cycle

The scene needs a square grid, and only one map can run at a time. In the combat tracker, create an encounter, set its objectives, then press Begin Encounter. Play opens on the Player Phase of round 1, where Lords, Retainers and Allies act, followed by the Enemy Phase, where Enemies and Bosses act. Within a phase, units act in any order. The round goes up each time play returns to the Player Phase, and every unit's actions and movement refresh at the start of its side's phase.

The tracker shows the round, how many units have acted, and your controls as the GM:

  • End Phase passes play to the other side (click twice to confirm). With Auto-Advance on, the phase passes by itself once the last unit has acted.

  • End Encounter ends the map as a success or a failure, or pauses it. A paused map resumes on the Player Phase of the round it was paused in.

  • The round number can be clicked to change it. Combat Music plays each phase's track, set in the Terrain Builder.

  • Free Exploration lets units move freely outside an encounter, without phases.

Movement and Actions

Each turn, a unit has a Standard Action, a Bonus Action and its Movement. Its turn is over once its Standard Action and Movement are both spent. Attacking, most spells and abilities, crossing terrain, and taking off or landing all use the Standard Action. Using a Bonus Action item or trading spends the unit's remaining movement, but leaves its Standard Action available.

To act with a unit, first take it up. Its weapons, spells, abilities and items then show up on its hotbar at the bottom of the screen. The unit acts from the square it's standing on, so move it into position first.

Using the hotbar. Click a hotbar slot, or press its key (see @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.t03al1QkHOCBns0f#controls/keybindings]{Controls/Keybindings}). What happens next depends on the item:

  • Weapons and attack spells. The squares the unit can reach are highlighted. Click an enemy in range to open the Combat Preview, which shows both sides' damage, hit and critical chances and the order of attacks, much like Fire Emblem's battle forecast. From there, the attacker can switch weapon or damage type, and click an attack in the order to skip it. Press Attack to begin the exchange.

  • Other spells, staves, abilities and consumables. An item that only affects its user goes straight to the Confirm Effect window. An item that targets units highlights its range; click the units you want to affect, up to the item's limit. Once the last target is picked, or after clicking a picked unit again or pressing Space to confirm fewer, the Confirm Effect window opens. An item that targets the ground asks for a square instead. Press Confirm to use the item.

  • Rally. Each ally that can be Rallied shows the Support rank the Rally would land at (see @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.EKqsPYVWwd9HQqoq#support]{Support}).

  • Shields and accessories. Pressing the slot equips or unequips the item.

Press Shift or Escape at any point to back out of targeting, or press Cancel in a window to go back to aiming.

Attacks and counters. Attacks in an exchange alternate between attacker and defender. A 4 Spd lead earns one extra attack, and an 8 Spd lead earns two. The defender counterattacks if its weapon has uses left and its range reaches the attacker.

Trading. With a unit taken up, press G (Trade) or the Trade button on its HUD. Every friendly unit next to it on the same level is marked; click one to open the trade window, then choose what each unit gives and confirm. Equipped items can't be traded, and both units need room for what they receive. During an encounter, trading spends the unit's Bonus Action and remaining movement; outside an encounter, it's free.

Loot and chests. Move onto a Loot pile or an unlocked chest and press F (Interact) to take items from it. Units can also put items into chests. Looting uses no action, but it locks in the unit's move to that square.

Ending a turn. Press End Turn on the HUD, or choose Move and End when confirming a move. A unit that ends its turn this way rests and recovers Stance. Some units can act further: Canter lets a unit move again with its remaining movement after attacking, and an Extra Action restores the unit's actions and movement once.

Flying. A flying unit uses Ascend or Land on the HUD, which takes its Standard Action and ends its turn. In the air, it ignores terrain costs and height, and flies over obstacles. A flier whose Stance breaks falls to the ground.

Zone Crossing

Maps can be split into zones at different heights, shown as Lv on the map. A unit can't just walk up or down a ledge unless the edge allows it. Instead, it attempts a crossing:

  • While you plan a move, small arrows on square edges mark where a crossing is possible. Their colour shows the chance of success, from green (very likely) to red (unlikely).

  • Moving through an arrow opens the Cross Terrain dialog, which shows the skill, the DC and the success rate. Climbing uses Athletics and descending uses Finesse, at DC 5 per level of height unless the map says otherwise.

  • The unit has to be on foot, not mounted, not Stance Broken, and have its Standard Action and at least 1 square of movement left.

  • A crossing ends the unit's turn without resting, pass or fail. A failed climb leaves the unit where it was. A failed descent still drops the unit, but it takes fall damage based on its max HP, the height of the fall and how badly the check failed.

Movement Commitment

Only one unit can be moved at a time on a map. To take up a unit, hover it and press Space, right-click it, or press Tab to cycle units. Then walk it with the movement keys or drag it along the highlighted squares. A unit can pass through an ally's square, but can't stop on it.

Press Space (or Move on the HUD) to confirm. Confirm Move locks in the move so far and keeps the unit selected; Move and End locks it in and ends the turn. Movement spent across confirmed moves adds up.

Press Shift or Escape, or double-click empty ground, to cancel. Before any move is confirmed, cancelling returns the unit to its starting square. After a confirm, it can only go back to the last confirmed square. Attacking, crossing terrain or ending the turn makes the move final.

Damage and Mitigation

Every hit deals damage to the target's HP, and Brk damage to its Stance. Def and Res reduce HP damage, and the armor a unit wears decides which damage types it's Protected against or Vulnerable to.

Stance Mechanics

Each hit deals Break (Brk) damage to the target's Stn, set by the attacker's weapon or spell. Brk damage comes in whole numbers or half-points, like 0.5 or 1.5.

At 0 Stn, the unit is Stance Broken:

  • It can't attack, use items, counterattack or cross terrain, though it can still move. If it's broken mid-exchange, it loses its remaining attacks.

  • It takes -4 to Mgt, Agi, Tqn, Wit and Cha.

  • It loses the Def and Res bonuses from its worn Armor, and from any Shield it has equipped.

  • A flier falls to the ground and can't take off again until it recovers. Melee units can start attacks against it while it's on the ground.

A unit regains Stance simply by ending its turn without taking an action. This restores Stance by a hidden stat, Stn Regen (3 by default), and a Stance Broken unit that ends its turn this way recovers all of its Stn. Healing that restores Stn works too. Stance Break ends as soon as Stn rises above 0. A unit whose Stn is brought back above 0 by an outside source before it has taken its turn gets its Action and Bonus Action back.

Damage Types

Every attack deals one damage type, which decides whether Def or Res reduces it:

  • Physical, reduced by Def: Slashing, Piercing, Crushing and Missile. Untyped damage, like an unarmed attack, also counts as physical.

  • Magical, reduced by Res: Fire, Ice, Lightning, Wind, Arcane, Decay, Shadow and Holy.

Some weapons can deal more than one type, like a dagger that deals Slashing up close and Missile when thrown. The Combat Preview lets the attacker choose between the types the weapon can deal; left to itself, it avoids types the target is immune to and goes for ones it's vulnerable to. A few spells, like Chaos Orb, pick a type at random on each hit.

Damage over time from statuses works differently: Bleeding is untyped and can't be reduced, while Poison and Corpse Rot deal Decay damage.

Vulnerabilities and Protections

Armor can be protected against, or vulnerable to, particular damage types. Statuses and features can add protections, vulnerabilities and immunities of their own.

  • Protection. The armor's Def or Res counts twice against that type, and the hit's Brk is capped at 1 (half a point if exactly 1 would get through).

  • Vulnerability. The hit deals double Brk, and struck armor loses two uses instead of one. HP damage isn't increased.

  • Immunity. The target takes no damage and no Brk of that type.

  • No armor. A unit wearing no armor counts as vulnerable to every damage type, so unarmored units are easy to Stance Break.

  • Broken armor. Armor at 0 uses gives half its Def and Res, loses its protections, and leaves the wearer vulnerable to every type it didn't already protect against.

The Combat Preview marks a damage type the target is protected against in red, and one it's vulnerable to in green. A Stance Broken unit loses its armor's damage type protections, and its Def and Res bonuses, until it recovers.

Damage Calculation

A weapon hit is worked out in this order:

  1. Attack. The weapon or spell's Atk, which may include dice, plus its scaling stat (see @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.EKqsPYVWwd9HQqoq#derived-stats]{Atk}).

  2. Effectiveness. If the weapon is effective against one of the target's unit types (like a bow against a Flying unit), every die and number in the Atk is doubled before anything else: 1d8+5 becomes 2d8+10. Against a target that's also Impervious, the multiplier is x1.35 instead of x2, rounded up.

  3. Mitigation. The target's Def (physical) or Res (magical) is subtracted, with the armor's part doubled if it's protected against the type. There's no minimum: a hit that doesn't beat the target's Def or Res deals 0.

  4. Critical hit. On a critical, the damage that got through is multiplied by the attacker's Crit Dmg: x2, plus 0.05 for each point of Tqn, rounded up. So a unit with 10 Tqn deals x2.5.

  5. Shields. Shield points soak up the damage before HP does. A hit absorbed entirely by Shields deals no Brk.

Critical chance is the attacker's Crit minus the target's Cha and its armor's Crit Reduction, as a percentage; a Marked target gives every attacker +10. Some features change criticals further, like one that halves the target's Def on a critical. The world setting To Player Crit Dmg. Multiplier lets you scale down the extra damage that criticals deal to Lords and Retainers.

Spells and abilities that deal damage are reduced by Def and Res the same way, unless they say otherwise. Their criticals use a flat x2, applied before Def or Res.

Wear. Each landed blow costs the attacker's weapon one use, and a weapon that breaks mid-exchange ends that unit's attacks. Each hit that deals damage costs the target's armor one use.

Defeat. A unit at 0 HP is defeated and removed from the map, and any loot it carries drops. A unit with an Extra Life spends it instead, and comes back at full HP and Stance. Destructible objects take no HP damage; attacks wear down their Integrity by the attacker's Brk.

Terrain Mechanics

Each square of a map can carry terrain, which you set up in the Terrain Builder (see @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.ZxXYJlf5ACElkTNj]{Using the Terrain Builder}). Press the Show Terrain Tips key (E by default) to see what each square does.

  • Move Cost. Most squares cost 1 movement to enter; rough terrain costs more. Airborne units ignore move costs.

  • Obstacle and Impassable. Ground units can't enter either. Fliers can cross Obstacles, but not Impassable squares.

  • Eva, Def and Res. A unit standing on the square gains or loses these stats. Airborne units don't.

  • Tile effects. A square can heal or damage the unit standing on it at the start of its side's phase. Damage from terrain leaves Lords and Retainers at 1 HP, unless the square is set to be lethal.

  • Exceptions. A square can exempt certain units, like Undead or Flying units, from its stats, cost or effects.

  • Restrictions. A square can forbid mounted or flying units, and a map can forbid flying or mounts altogether.

Height gives no bonus to hit or damage. What it does is limit reach: melee and touch-range actions can only reach 1 level up or down, unless the attacker is airborne.

Line of Sight Rules

Attacks and most abilities need a clear line from the user to the target. Each item sets its rule under Line of Sight:

  • Normal. Walls block the line, and so does raised terrain more than 1 level above it. A target is only hidden if every line to it is blocked.

  • Ignore Elev. Walls still block, but height doesn't. Rally works this way.

  • Ignore LoS. Nothing blocks it. Long-range spells like Call Lightning and Purge work this way.

Units don't block line of sight, and height checks are skipped when either unit is airborne. Squares blocked only by height still show on the attack grid, dimmed, because flying units there can still be hit. Under the default Flyer Targeting setting (Aerial), a unit on the ground can't hit a flier with melee unless the flier is Stance Broken. As the GM, you can toggle on or off line-of-sight checking for one unit with the Free Targeting button on its token HUD. This is in case you want to allow a player character or NPC to override the game system's native LoS tracking, or if you think the way the game is doing LoS is not quite right for a certain scenario.

Vision. Units see 5 squares by default, plus any Sight bonus; Blinded units see only 1. Walls block vision, but terrain doesn't. Lords and Retainers share vision with their party. While a move is being planned, vision stays on the last confirmed square, so previewing a path doesn't reveal anything. Fog of war, token vision and the Map Visible option are set per scene in the Terrain Builder.

Enemy Automation

With the Enemy AI module, the Enemy Phase can be played for you. Each unit's behaviour is set in the Combat AI tab of its Actor Control Panel (see @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.4bL4mJsYfkVkFUxV]{Configuring Enemy AI}).

Turning It On or Off

Once an encounter is created, the combat tracker shows an Enemy AI button below Auto-Advance. Only the GM and Assistant GMs see it. Each press moves it to the next of three modes:

  • Off. You play the Enemy Phase yourself. A new encounter starts in this mode.

  • On (white border). The AI plays the next Enemy Phase, then switches itself off when the Player Phase begins.

  • Locked (gold border and padlock icon). The AI plays every Enemy Phase until you switch it off.

The mode is kept with the encounter, including through a pause. Switching the AI on during an Enemy Phase starts it right away. Double-click the button to turn it on and lock it at once; otherwise, it turns itself off again at the next Player Phase. This gives you fine control over when to use enemy automation: you might want to play a few enemies by hand before letting the AI handle the rest.

How It Works

The AI runs on the host client when the Enemy Phase begins. It plays the enemy units that are alive and visible on the map; tokens hidden in Foundry are treated as not having arrived yet.

  • Turn order. Units with a higher Priority (set in the unit's Actor Control Panel) act first. After that, Aggressive and Berserk units act early, and Cautious, Defensive and Support units act late.

  • Each turn. The camera follows the unit as it acts. It moves, then attacks or uses a healing item, choosing targets according to its profile. A unit with nothing to attack may roam, pursue or head for a Defense Point, as its conditions direct. The AI ends each unit's turn itself.

  • Manual units. The AI never plays a unit set to Manual. When it reaches one, it waits for you to play that unit and end its turn, then carries on.

  • The map is held. While the AI plays, nobody else can move units.

  • End of the phase. The AI doesn't end the phase. With Auto-Advance on, the phase passes once every unit has acted; otherwise, press End Phase.

Stopping the AI Mid-Phase

Press the Enemy AI button again, or press Space twice quickly on the host client. The button works even while the map is busy.

  • The action under way, like a move or an attack, finishes and isn't undone. The AI then stops and switches itself off.

  • If a unit was mid-turn, you'll get a notification, and you finish its turn yourself. Units the AI hadn't reached yet still get their turn, and you can turn the AI back on at any time.

Reloading. If the host client reloads or closes during an AI-played Enemy Phase, it asks when it comes back whether to resume the Enemy AI for the units still to act. Answering 'No' leaves them to you.

Uncertain results. If the AI can't confirm the result of an action, it stops for the rest of that phase and names the unit for you to check. The remaining units then have to be played by hand.

Threat Indicators

During an encounter, selecting a unit draws a line to it from every hostile unit that could reach its square on its next turn. The lines update as the unit moves, so a path can be checked square by square before it's confirmed. Players can also click a unit they don't control to inspect its threats.

With the Enemy AI module, selecting or inspecting an enemy shows a single line to the unit it plans to attack this turn instead. Keep in mind that this line only shows what the AI would do. You may decide to operate that unit by hand instead, so players have the right to ask you whether a threat indicator is reliable, that is, whether you'll be controlling that unit yourself.

A line's colour shows how much harm one hit would do. Hit chance isn't counted.

  • Grey. The hostile can't attack: it's Stance Broken, Stunned, Frozen, Feared or in Stasis.

  • Thin orange. A minor threat. An average hit may deal a middling amount of HP or Stance damage.

  • Red. A severe threat. An average hit would take more than 30% of the unit's current HP, or the hostile's best possible hit would defeat it.

  • Thick red. An average hit would defeat its target.

Combat Tracker

Once an encounter is created, the combat tracker in the sidebar shows the encounter in place of Foundry's initiative list. The sidebar tab turns blue during the Player Phase, red during the Enemy Phase, and green during Free Exploration.

Reading the Tracker

  • Toggles. Auto-Advance, Combat Music and Enemy AI sit at the top.

  • Phase panel. The round, followed by the round limit if the objectives set one (Round 3/10), the current phase, and how many of that side's units have acted.

  • Roster. Player and Enemy tabs, each with a count of living units. The tracker shows the acting side until another tab is clicked. Sort cycles between name, HP, loot, aura, type and turn, and the arrow beside it sets the direction. Objective and protected units are always listed first. Neutral units aren't listed, and players only see the enemies their units can see.

  • Each row. The unit's portrait, ringed in its faction colour, its name, an HP bar, and one shield per point of Stance, orange while it remains.

  • Clicking a row pans the camera to the unit, and for the GM, also selects it. Double-clicking opens its sheet.

Symbols

  • Crown. A Lord.

  • Gold trophy. A unit that has to be defeated to win the map. Its row is tinted gold.

  • Blue shield. A protected unit: losing it loses the map. Its row is tinted blue.

  • Gold chequered flag. The unit has reached an Arrival Point.

  • Sack. Green: drops loot when defeated. Red: carries stealable items. Yellow: both.

  • Blue broadcast tower. The unit is emitting an aura.

  • Footprints (GM only, Enemy AI). The unit's current movement order: red for Pursue, yellow for Free Roam, white for Seize.

  • Green check, faded row. The unit has acted this phase.

  • Grey, faded row. The unit has been defeated.

Finishing A Map

A map is either automatically completed when an encounter meets the win condition(s) set by the GM via the Set Objectives menu, or when it meets the fail condition(s). The GM may also manually end a map via the Combat Tracker's buttons.

When finishing a map, all items marked as 'Refreshes' should regain their uses, but this will not happen automatically. The GM has to grant this via the GM macro 'Restore All Units (Scene)' or '(World)'. This is so that GMs have total control as to when units actually regain their resources, in case, for whatever reason, the GM does not judge that the units may recover their spell or ability Refreshes just yet.

Death and Defeat

When any unit hits 0 HP, they fade off the map.

Whether or not a unit permanently dies when their HP hits 0 is up to you as the GM, and the players must have the right to know what are the terms of permadeath. For insance, you might declare at the start of a map that only the first Retainer or Lord to perish on the map will suffer permadeath. All other units who hit 0 HP retreat, get a stat/level penalty, or some other consequence of the GM's judgment. In my own campaign I generally blanket declare all Retainers as being subject to permadeath when their HP hits 0, but I gave the Lord units more grace. You may also give the players some kind of macguffin, like a one-time resurrection potion, as a way for them to mulligan deaths. This can be especially handy for newer players who are still getting the hang of this kind of gameplay.

What is Downtime?

Downtime is the time between maps, when the party rests, recovers and gets ready for the next battle. It's also where a lot of a unit's growth happens: forging gear, cooking meals that raise growth rates, and building Supports. For how Downtime fits into a campaign, see @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.CgEUqW0uzVMKrBdY#structure-of-play]{Structure of Play}.

As the GM, you start Downtime by pressing Free Exploration in the combat tracker. Units can then move freely around the scene, with no turns or movement limits, and use the scene's stations. During Free Exploration, units can only use Potions, Boosters, Promotions and Mounts, and can't steal or fire Armaments.

Starting Free Exploration refills every unit's Energy and Downtime Action. When the party is done, press Reset Downtime. That restores every unit's Energy and Downtime Action too, and it also ends meal and performance bonuses, unlocks requisitioned factions, and makes vendors forget haggles and buybacks. Right-clicking a unit in the tracker lets you reset that unit alone, or give it back some Energy.

Energy Costs

Each downtime, a unit can do either several small activities with its Energy, or one bigger activity with its Downtime Action, but not both.

  • Energy. Every unit has 3 Energy. Gathering, Forging, Alchemy and picking a lock cost 1 Energy each. A unit that spends its last Energy is Exhausted.

  • Downtime Action. Cooking, Performing, Requisitioning, Haggling, Socializing and Training each use the unit's whole Downtime Action, leaving it Exhausted.

A unit that has started spending Energy can't take a Downtime Action, and the other way around. Energy activities grant a little skill XP for each Energy spent; Downtime Actions grant more all at once.

Forging

At a Workshop, a unit restores a damaged weapon's or armor's durability with a skill check. The item has to allow forging, and it has to be carried by the unit or kept in the party's Convoy. Each attempt costs 1 Energy and the item's listed materials, which are taken from the unit's pockets first, then the Convoy. There's no DC: the durability restored equals the roll, times the item's forge multiplier.

Every point of durability restored adds 1 Forging XP to the item. Once it has enough, the item is refined to its next tier, up to +5, and its name shows the tier, like Iron Sword (+1). Each tier improves the item however its author set it up: a weapon might gain Atk, Acc, Crit or durability, or lose weight; armor might gain Def, Res, Stn or a protection. A refined item is also worth more.

Alchemy

At a Laboratory, a unit crafts Potions and Bombs, or repairs staves. Every Potion or Bomb with a list of required materials can be crafted, and no recipes need to be learned. Crafting costs 1 Energy and the materials, and rolls the item's skill (Nature by default) against its DC:

  • A total that doesn't beat the DC fails, and the materials are still spent.

  • A total above the DC makes one.

  • A total of 6 or more above the DC makes two.

The finished item goes to the unit's pockets, or to the Convoy when its pockets are full. Repairing a staff works like Forging, but staves can't be refined.

Gathering

At a Gathering Node, like a mine, a fishing spot or a tree to fell, a unit gathers Resources with a skill check (Athletics, unless the node says otherwise). There's no DC: the amount gathered is the roll times the node's multiplier, drawn at random from what the node holds, with common resources more likely than rare ones. Each attempt costs 1 Energy. The haul goes to the Convoy or the unit's inventory, whichever the player picks. A node that runs out is removed from the map.

Chests/Locks

Locked chests and doors can be opened in two ways:

  • Key. A unit carrying the lock's key opens it outright. The key is used up.

  • Lockpicking. A unit with the Locktouch ability can pick the lock with a Handicraft check against its DC. A lock with DC 0 only opens with its key.

Stand on a chest, or next to a door, and press Interact (F). During Free Exploration, each lockpicking attempt costs 1 Energy, pass or fail, and a failed lock can be tried again while the unit has Energy left. During an encounter, an attempt takes the unit's Standard Action and ends its turn. An opened chest shows its contents to take.

Cooking

At a Cooking Pot, a unit cooks a meal for itself and any party members it invites to eat. The chef uses its Downtime Action, but the diners don't. The meal needs the recipe's ingredients for every diner, and the chef rolls Nature against the recipe's DC:

  • Well Fed (total above the DC). Every diner gains the recipe's growth rate bonuses.

  • Sated Stomach (failed). Every diner gains half the bonuses, rounded down.

  • Envigorated (5 or more above the DC, with a special ingredient). As Well Fed, and every diner also gains +1 to a stat set by the special ingredient's food type, like Meat for Mgt or Fruit for Cha.

The growth bonuses apply to the diners' level-ups until you reset Downtime (see @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.EKqsPYVWwd9HQqoq#growth-rates]{Growth Rates}). Each unit can eat one meal per downtime. The chef and each diner also gain Support XP together: 5 for a failed meal, 10 for a success and 15 with a special ingredient.

Every Cooking Pot offers the default recipes in the Recipe Library. You can add personal recipes, and teach one to a unit by dragging it onto the Notes tab of the unit's character sheet.

Inspired and Uninspired units can't perform or hear another song until then. Performers and listeners also gain Support XP with one another.

Every Instrument offers the default songs in the Song Library. You can add personal songs, and teach one to a unit by dragging it onto the Notes tab of its character sheet.

Requisitioning

At a Stationary, a unit asks one of the factions you've listed there for funds, using its Downtime Action. The unit chooses how much gold to ask for, in steps of 100 GP up to the faction's wealth, and rolls Civics. The DC is set by the faction's relation to the party (Poor 15, Neutral 10, Decent 7, Friendly 5, Devoted 0), plus 1 for every 100 GP asked.

On a success, the gold is sent to the party's Convoy as inbound gold for you to deliver; the unit needs a linked Convoy to requisition at all. Win or lose, that faction can't be asked again until you reset Downtime. Only gold can be requisitioned for now.

Socializing

Two units of the same party can spend time together to build their Support. With nothing to interact with, press Interact (F) next to a party member and click it, then choose Socialize. Both units roll Sociability, and their bond gains Support XP equal to the two totals added together (see @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.EKqsPYVWwd9HQqoq#support]{Support}). Both units use their Downtime Action.

Training

From the same window, choose Train and pick a weapon proficiency. The unit with the higher rank in it trains the other. The trainer rolls Command, and the student gains proficiency XP equal to the total (see @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.EKqsPYVWwd9HQqoq#proficiency-xp]{Proficiency XP}). Both units also gain a little level XP, as from a sparring match, and 5 Support XP together. Both units use their Downtime Action.

Praying

Praying at Altars isn't implemented yet, and will come in a future update.

Buying From Vendors

The shop window both buys and sells, switched with Switch to Selling and Switch to Buying. With Send to Convoy ticked (the default), bought goods go straight to the party's Convoy and are paid from the unit's purse first, then the Convoy's gold. Unticked, they go to the unit, and only its purse pays.

Worn items, like a weapon with few uses left, sell for less.

Setting Up a Vendor

The vendor's sheet holds its stock and its gold:

  • Stock. Drag items onto the sheet to stock them. Each item's In Stock field sets how many are for sale: blank means unlimited, and 0 means sold out.

  • GP. The vendor's own gold. It grows as the party buys and shrinks as it pays for goods. A vendor short of gold only pays what it has, and the seller is warned first.

  • Clear Stock (sheet header) removes every item from the vendor at once. Right-click an item to lock it, and Clear Stock will keep it.

  • Linked Actor. When ticked, every token of this vendor shares one stock and purse.

What the vendor buys. Press Merchandise Settings in the sheet header and tick the kinds of goods the vendor will buy from players: Weapon, Staff, Armor, Shield, Accessory, Potion, Bomb, Booster, Promotion, Material, Textile, Reagent, Ingredient and Miscellaneous. A blacksmith might only buy weapons and armor, while an apothecary buys potions and reagents. Goods the vendor doesn't accept can't be sold to it, and items marked as untradeable can't be sold to any vendor.

Buying back. Goods a party sells stay on the vendor's shelf, and that party can buy them back for the same price it was paid. A vendor won't buy back an item it sold until you reset Downtime.

The Token Studio, titled Emblem Character Studio in its window, is where you build and edit a unit's portrait and map sprites in GBA-style pixel art, the way the Fire Emblem games of that era drew them. It comes with the Emblem RPG Studio module, which also needs socketlib.

The GM and Assistant GMs can edit any Character, Vendor or Convoy. Trusted Players can edit the actors they own, if you allow them under Configure Settings, Trusted Player Studio Access, Choose Trusted Players. A Trusted Player's saves are written through the host client, so the GM has to be connected. Compendium actors can't be edited.

There are three ways in:

  • Press the Emblem Character Studio button (palette icon) in the Token controls, then drag an actor from the sidebar onto the window.

  • Press Edit beside any token slot in a unit's Actor Control Panel, which opens the studio straight on that slot.

  • Click a Vendor's portrait on its sheet.

You can load several units at once and switch between them from the footer; right-click one to unload the others. The window's header has a Control Panel button for the loaded unit and an Expand / Restore button.

How the Studio Works

  • Each tab has two panes side by side: Avatar (the portrait) on the left and Token (the map sprite) on the right. Each pane is a 128 by 128 pixel canvas with a layer list, a toolbar above it, and a rail of trays beside it: Colour, the parts trays, Export and Import. Either pane can be hidden from the controls row.

  • A sprite is a stack of Layers. Every pixel tool only works on the selected layer, so pick a layer in the layer list before you paint. The top row of the list is the frontmost layer.

  • Sprites are assembled from Parts: template pieces in the trays, such as a Body, a Face or an Idle pose. Clicking a part adds it as a new layer. The shipped parts are read-only; your own parts live in the Parts Library at worlds/<world>/emblem/parts/.

  • A layer is either Linked or Rasterized, shown by the chain icon on its row. A Linked layer follows a colour palette: each pixel remembers which palette colour and shade it is, so changing the palette recolours the whole part at once. E.g. set the Hair row to red and every hair pixel turns red, with its shading kept. Parts from the trays are Linked. A Rasterized layer is plain pixels with fixed colours: uploaded images, blank layers and merged layers.

  • A unit can have many sprites: one per class it can be, per type it can become (Mounted, Flying and so on) and per battle moment (On Attack, On Crit). Each studio tab edits one of these. The Default | Default tab is always open, and the portrait can only be edited and saved from that tab.

  • Save writes the pane to the unit as a 128 by 128 PNG in worlds/<world>/emblem/character/<unit>/, and tokens on the map and open sheets update straight away, for every player. The studio also keeps each sprite's layers with the actor, so you can reopen and change it later.

  • The Outline row of every palette is the colour the system looks for when a scene recolours token outlines (the Token Outline Colour world setting, #382040 by default). Keep outlines in that one colour: art outlined in any other shade is left as it is on every map.

Building a Sprite

To build a portrait from parts

  1. Load the unit and stay on the Default | Default tab.

  2. In the Avatar pane, open the Body tray and click a body. It's added as a layer.

  3. Click a Face, then a Hair. Adding a Hair part also adds its matching Hair Back part behind it.

  4. Add an Accessory if you want one.

  5. Press Shadow. It paints a soft shadow onto the face where the hair meets the skin, and follows later skin colour changes.

While the canvas holds just one untouched part of a kind, clicking another part of that kind swaps it in and keeps its colours, so you can flip through bodies or hairstyles quickly. Drag a part onto the canvas to always add it as a new layer instead.

To make the token sprite

  1. In the Token pane, open the FECC tray, which holds the full set of shipped map sprites, and click the one that fits the unit's class. The Idle, Dodge, Attack, WEAP, Parts and Effects trays hold the pieces those sprites are built from, split into sub-tabs by weapon: Default, Sword, Spear, Heavy, Covert, Bow, Magic and Creature.

  2. Press HP/Stn bar guide and check that nothing important sits in the shaded strip at the bottom.

  3. Press Preview token at map scale to see it at the size it'll be on the map.

The thumbnails in every tray are drawn in the pane's current colours, so a recoloured palette shows on the parts before you add them.

To recolour a part

The Colour tray edits a palette. With a Linked layer selected, it edits that layer's own palette, so recolouring one part leaves the others alone. With no layer selected, it edits the tab's default palette, which new parts start with.

  1. Select the layer in the layer list.

  2. Open the Colour tray. On the avatar the rows are Hair, Eye, Skin, Metal, Trim, Cloth, Leather and Accessory; on the token they're Palette 1 to Palette 8. An Outline row comes last. Each row has five shades, Lighter, Light mid, Neutral, Dark mid and Darker, and Skin has two darker ones besides. Shades the layer doesn't use are greyed out.

  3. Left-click a shade to change its colour, or press Show Prefabs on the row for a ready-made set of shades. Asset Default restores the colours the part was saved with.

  4. To give every sprite of the unit the same colours, press the bullhorn button in the tray's header and choose Broadcast to All or Broadcast to Tokens Only. It copies this palette onto every Linked layer of every open tab.

Right-click a shade to load it into the brush. A row can be copied and pasted onto another row, the header can copy and paste a whole palette, and the dice button rolls a random set of colours for every row. Painting on a Linked layer keeps it Linked: the brush paints the nearest palette colour, so the pixels you paint change with the palette too.

To recolour an image that isn't a part

An uploaded picture or a merged layer has no palette. For those, the Colour tray becomes Recolour, which swaps individual colours.

  1. Select the Rasterized layer. The tray lists every distinct colour in it.

  2. Click a colour's original swatch to make those pixels pulse on the canvas, so you can see where it's used.

  3. Click its New colour swatch to change it, or the reset button to put it back. With part of the layer selected, changes only apply to the selected pixels.

The header can reset every colour, or copy this set of changes and apply it to another layer, where it's matched to the nearest original colours. The layer stays Rasterized, and each change can be undone. To turn a Linked layer into plain pixels, click its chain icon and confirm Rasterize layer?; its colours are baked in and it can no longer be swapped from the trays. Merging a layer into the one below rasterizes the result too. The only way back to a Linked layer is the Import tray.

To save the sprite to the unit

  1. Press Save in the pane's toolbar. The Avatar pane saves the portrait and the Token pane saves the tab's token slot. The footer shows the file each tab will save to, and its Prefix field sets a different start to the file names.

  2. Or press Save All to save every open tab at once. It warns you first if any emptied pane would remove saved art.

Files are named after the unit, class, type and condition, like hugo-paladin-mounted-default.png. Saving an empty canvas offers to remove that saved art, though the file stays on disk. A dot on a tab marks unsaved changes, and the studio remembers your open units, tabs and unsaved work a few seconds after each edit, so closing the window and reopening it resumes where you left off.

Class and Battle Variants

On the map, the system shows the sprite for the unit's current Class item and type, with any matching condition on top. A class with no sprite of its own falls back to the unit's base sprite, so a unit only needs the variants you care to draw. For instance, a Cavalier might have just a Default sprite and a Mounted one, plus an On Crit sprite for the cut-in.

Each tab's destination is set by three selectors above the canvases, confirmed with Submit:

  • Class. Default is the unit's base sprite. Each class tab in the unit's Actor Control Panel adds its own row. Class tabs have to be named exactly after the Class item, and the studio follows renamed class tabs automatically.

  • Type. Default, Armored, Mounted, Armored Mounted or Flying: used when the unit is in Heavy armor, mounted, both, or in the air. The Default class only has the Default type.

  • Entry. An optional condition set up in the Control Panel. Some last while they're true: Unarmed, Wielding a Blade or another weapon type, Wielding a Specific Item, or Using an Ability. Others swap the sprite for a moment: On Attack, On Crit, On Cast and On Evade.

The tab strip lists Default and each class on its top row, with an extra row for each type that has art, like Paladin: Mounted. The tabs below carry short labels like Def, Atk, Crit, Cast, Ddg or Wld: Bl; hover one for its full name. Class tabs, conditions, token scales and height offsets are added and changed in the Actor Control Panel, which you can open from the studio's header.

To add a sprite for a class, a type or a battle moment

  1. Press + on a class row of the tab strip. A blank tab opens.

  2. Pick its Class, Entry and Type, and press Submit. The tab now has a destination, shown in the footer. A new class tab starts from the Default sprite's layers.

  3. Build the sprite as usual. For a battle moment, the Attack, Dodge and Effects trays hold the poses and flashes.

  4. Press Save.

If the destination already has art, saving asks whether to Overwrite it, Layer the saved art in on top, or Purge the canvas and load the saved art. Open all saved token variants as tabs on the tab strip opens every saved sprite at once. Drag tabs to reorder them, and right-click a tab to close it, close the others, or close all.

Importing Your Own Art

Uploading a picture gives you a Rasterized layer, which is fine for a one-off portrait. To get a part you can recolour from the palette and reuse on other units, run it through the Sprite Importer instead, which assigns each of the picture's colours to a palette shade.

To turn your own art into a recolourable part

  1. In the Import tray, press Open Importer, then Add File or paste an image with Ctrl+V. Open From Layer imports the selected layer instead, placing the result as a Linked layer above it; Open From Tab and Open From All Tabs import whole canvases.

  2. Drag each of the image's colours, listed on the left, onto a shade chip on the right, from lighter to darker: Outline, Palette 1 (Hair), Palette 2 (Wild Card 1), Palette 3 (Skin), Palette 4 (Metal), Palette 5 (Trim), Palette 6 (Cloth), Palette 7 (Leather) or Palette 8 (Wild Card 2). Drop a colour on Remove to cut it out, like a background.

  3. Where one colour serves two things, such as a grey used for both armour and a blade, Alt+drag places only one connected patch of it.

  4. Press Auto-classify Rest to assign whatever is left, or Reset to start over. A colour you place once is placed in every image in the importer.

  5. Tick Save to library to keep the part, then press Import. You're asked to name it.

The part lands on the canvas as a Linked layer and, if saved, appears in its tray for every unit. Import stays disabled until every colour is placed. Images can be up to 256 by 256 pixels with at most 64 colours, and the visible art after removals at most 192 by 192. A 248 by 160 image is read as a cell from a Fire Emblem character creator sheet: its top rows are trimmed and its green background removed for you.

Naming. The ? button in the importer posts the naming rules to your chat. Names can use letters, digits, - and _, and a blank name saves as custom_assetN. The name decides where the part is filed:

  • Token parts go to a tray by the name's last word: effect or fx to Effects; attack, atk, crit or cast to Attack; weapon or wep to Weapons; dodge, evade or ddg to Dodge; part to Parts; anything else to Idle. A weapon word anywhere in the name files Idle, Dodge and Attack parts under a sub-tab: sword or blade, spear, lance or pole, axe or heavy, covert, bow, magic, or monster, creature, beast or undead. E.g. soldier-pole-idle goes to Idle, under Spear.

  • Avatar parts go to a tray by a slot word: hair-back or hb, accessory or acc, face or head, hair, or body, armor or outfit (Body is the default). E.g. Lyn_Hair goes to Hair.

If a name is taken, choose Overwrite, Append Number or Rename. Shipped parts can't be overwritten.

To organise your parts

Your own parts can be moved and sorted however you like; the shipped parts stay where they are. Right-click a part for:

  • Copy to my library, on a shipped part, copies it into your library, where you can move, rename and recolour it as a starting point.

  • Move to Sub-Tab files one of your parts under a sub-tab, or under the tray's Default or Custom entry to take it out of any sub-tab.

  • Move to Tray moves one of your parts to another tray on the same side, for example from Idle to Attack.

  • Rename and Delete. Delete hides the part from the trays, but its file stays on disk.

Press + in a tray to make a sub-tab of your own, such as one per unit or per faction; right-click a sub-tab to rename or delete it, and its parts return to Default or Custom. Each tray also has a search box and a toggle for 2, 3 or 4 thumbnails to a row.

Exporting, Projects and Spritesheets

To export a picture file

  1. Open the Export tray on the pane you want.

  2. Press a size: Raw (1x, 128 by 128), Tiny (2x), Small (10x) or Full (20x, 2560 by 2560).

The PNG is saved in worlds/<world>/emblem/export/, named after the unit, pane, size and time. Pixels are scaled cleanly with no blurring, and gridlines and guides are left out.

To back up or move a unit's work

A project file holds a whole session's work on a unit: every open tab with all its layers, colours, positions and destinations, plus the unit's class tabs, conditions, token scales and offsets. The pixels are stored inside the file, so it doesn't depend on any image files and can be loaded in another world.

  1. Press Save every tab as a project (floppy disk button), enter a project name, and confirm. It's saved as worlds/<world>/emblem/projects/<name>.json, and asks before overwriting one.

  2. To load one, press Load a project (folder button). It opens the projects folder, or a list of saved projects for players who can't browse files.

Loading only places the layers on the canvases; nothing is written to the actor until you save. Class tabs and conditions the project needs but the unit lacks are created in its Actor Control Panel, while anything already there keeps its own settings. Projects saved by older versions of the studio can't be loaded.

To lay a unit's sprites out on a spritesheet

A spritesheet is a large scratch canvas with a unit's token sprites on one grid: for an overview, a picture to share, or a batch of art to split back into parts. The game doesn't use spritesheets on the map.

  1. Press Create a spritesheet (grid button) on the Default row of the tab strip.

  2. Choose From Current Tab's Layers (one sprite per layer) or From All Tabs (one sprite per tab).

  3. Press Save Sheet to keep it with the unit. It's saved as <unit>-spritesheet.png and reopens whenever the unit is loaded.

Each sprite is trimmed to its visible pixels and laid out up to six to a row, on one layer named Spritesheet. Right-click the tab to rename it, and closing a saved sheet offers to keep it or delete it. Spritesheet tabs can't be bound to a token slot, and have no bar guide or map preview. The Export tray works on them up to 8192 pixels across.

  • Sending sprites to tabs. Select a sprite on the sheet with Rectangle Select or the Magic Wand, right-click the selection and choose a tab under Copy To. The pixels are copied into that tab's token canvas as a new layer without leaving the sheet.

  • Splitting a sheet. Import from Spritesheet in the Import tray finds each separate sprite on the sheet and runs it through the Sprite Importer, each landing as its own layer. Import to New Spritesheet in the importer does the reverse, placing a whole batch on a new sheet tab.

Notes

  • Where It's Saved. Sprites in worlds/<world>/emblem/character/<unit>/, your parts in worlds/<world>/emblem/parts/<tray>/, exports in worlds/<world>/emblem/export/, and projects in worlds/<world>/emblem/projects/.

  • Limits. Canvases are 128 by 128. Uploads up to 1024 pixels a side. Imports up to 256 by 256, 64 colours, 192 by 192 of visible art. Undo keeps 32 steps per canvas. Exports up to 8192 pixels a side.

The Terrain Builder is where you give a map its mechanics: movement costs, stat bonuses, hazards, heights, teleporters, objective points, reinforcements, lights, sounds and walls. A GM or Assistant GM opens it from the Terrain Builder group (mountain icon) in the Scene Controls. The scene needs a square grid. Choosing another control group, changing scene or closing the window closes it.

The window has three modes, chosen in its header: Terrain, for painting squares, Draw Walls, for drawing Foundry walls, and Settings, for options that apply to the whole scene. The control group also has Show Light Objects and Show Sound Objects toggles, which reveal the lights and sounds the builder places.

How Terrain Works

  • Terrain is saved on the scene, one record per square. Everything a square can carry is set by the trays down the left of the builder menu: Stats, Geo, Mech, FX, Audio, Light and Adv. The Overview tray lists what a square already has.

  • The trays are one form listing its possible parameters. Selecting squares loads the values they share into it, and Save to Squares writes the whole form of every tab into that square. E.g. if I make edits in the Stats tray and edits in the Geo tray, then Save to Square will write both those changes into the square.

  • Height comes only from Zones. A zone is a named group of squares at a given elevation level, and squares in no zone are at ground level (Elevation 0). Save to Squares never changes a square's zone or height; the zone tools do.

  • A preset is the form saved under a name. It holds everything except zone and height, so it can be reused on any map.

  • Players see what you've painted with the Show Terrain Tips key (E by default), which shows every square's effects. The only exception is a spawn marker, which is only shown to them if its array says so.

  • Squares you have authored and want to re-use ought to be saved as a Preset. For instance, if there is a specific way you want to handle 'forest' type Evasion bonus tiles, you should save that as a Preset and reuse it. Loading a Preset will not automatically overwrite your selected square(s), but will overwrite whatever parameters are currently entered into the builder's trays.

Selecting squares

In Terrain mode you select squares on the map, set their properties in the trays, and save them. Selections are always rectangles:

Input

Effect

Click, or drag

Selects one square, or a rectangle of squares, replacing the selection (blue).

Alt + drag

Adds a rectangle to the selection (green).

Ctrl + drag

Removes a rectangle from the selection (red).

Right-drag

Pans the map.

The footer shows how many squares are selected, and with one square, its row, column and height. A field the selected squares disagree on shows its default, and saving writes that default to all of them. To change one field on squares that differ, select them one at a time.

Lock (the padlock in the footer) keeps the current selection while you work, so a stray click on the map doesn't replace it. The zone buttons can still change it.

Painting squares

To set the terrain of some squares

  1. Select the squares.

  2. In the Stats tray, set the Eva, Def and Res a unit standing there gains or loses.

  3. In the Geo tray, set the Move Cost, or tick Obstacle or Impassable.

  4. Press Save to Squares.

Select one of the squares and the Overview tray lists what it now carries. Press the Show Terrain Tips key outside the builder to see it the way players will.

To copy one square's terrain to other squares

  1. Select the square and press Copy. The form is copied as it stands, unsaved changes included.

  2. Select the squares to paint.

  3. Press Paste. The form is filled in, but nothing is saved yet.

  4. Press Save to Squares.

To save terrain as a preset

  1. Fill in the trays, or select a square that already has the terrain you want.

  2. Press Save to Preset.

  3. Enter a Name, optionally Choose Icon, and press Save Preset.

Saving under the name of one of your presets replaces it without asking; clicking a preset in the dialog fills in its name and icon for that. The names of the shipped presets can't be used. Your presets are kept per world, in Data/worlds/<world>/json/terrain.json.

To paint a preset onto squares

  1. Select the squares.

  2. Press Load from Preset, pick one of the Default Presets (Fire Tile, Light Tile, Flasked Fire and Ichorous Pool) or your Custom Presets, and press Load. The form is filled in.

  3. Press Save to Squares.

The × on a custom preset deletes it. Shipped presets can't be deleted.

To clear squares

Clear wipes the selected squares completely, zone and height included. It doesn't ask, and it can't be undone.

Levels (Elevation)

As of right now (Emblem RPG v1.0.3), Foundry's native elevation mechanisms are unused. This may change in a future update when I integrate the game system with Foundry's native handling of Levels.

Rather, Elevation is currently a simple flag on a square's saved data. It changes how units move and fight: a unit on foot can't walk up or down between elevated platforms without a Skill check, melee only reaches one level up or down, and raised ground blocks sight. The rules players play by are under @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.fRmf6UOHviDS5kFI#zone-crossing]{Zone Crossing} and @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.fRmf6UOHviDS5kFI#terrain-mechanics]{Terrain Mechanics} on the Combat page. This is how you build those levels.

To raise squares to a new level

  1. Select the squares.

  2. Press New from Selection in the Zones pane. A zone named Zone appears, at level 0, in a colour unlike the others.

  3. With squares of the zone still selected, type a Name and set Elev to the level: 1 for one storey up.

  4. Press Update.

The zone is drawn on the map with a dashed outline in its colour and labelled Lv N, and every square in it is at that height. Squares taken from another zone leave it, and a zone left empty is deleted.

To change a zone

  • Add squares. Select them and press + on the zone's row. They move into the zone at its height.

  • Select all of its squares. Press the select button on its row.

  • Rename it, recolour it or move it to another level. Select squares inside it, change Name, Outline or Elev, and press Update. Changing Elev moves every square in the zone.

  • Take squares out. Select them and press Unlink selection. They return to ground level and keep their other terrain.

  • Delete it. Press Delete zone. It doesn't ask. Its squares return to ground level and keep their other terrain.

The Zones list is sorted from the highest level down. Squares in no zone are called the Ground Floor when units cross to them.

To make stairs between two levels

Both levels need to exist first.

  1. Select the stair squares on either side of the ledge.

  2. In the Geo tray, set Transition to Directional.

  3. Light the arrows for both ways across the ledge, or press All Directions. An arrow is the direction a unit travels, and it only has to be lit on one of the two squares a step joins.

  4. To keep riders or fliers off the stairs, set Type Restriction to Cannot be Mounted or Cannot be Flying. They can still stand on the square.

  5. Press Save to Squares.

A unit can freely now walk between the two zones through the transitional square(s). Edges you didn't light still ask for a crossing check.

To change how a ledge is crossed

By default, climbing rolls Athletics and descending rolls Finesse, at a DC of 5 per level of difference. For example, moving from Ground (0) to an Elevated Zone (Lv 4) would mean beating an Athletics check of DC 20 (4 * 5). To change that along a ledge, or to forbid such a crossing:

  1. Select the squares on one side of the ledge. Zone Crossing is only offered when a selected square has a neighbour at another height.

  2. In the Geo tray, set Transition to Zone Crossing.

  3. For each direction that leads to another height, choose the Skill: Athletics, Finesse, Either (whichever the unit is better at) or Disabled, which forbids crossing that way.

  4. Set the DC Mult. The DC is the multiplier times the levels of difference.

  5. Press Save to Squares.

The settings apply to units leaving these squares in those directions.

To make A Transition Between Obstacles

There may be some cases where you want to connect two Zones so that one is accessible by climbing from the other, but still want to have some obstacle between the two. You can create a connective bridge between the access point and the destination using the same method as prior.

  1. Select the squares the bridge runs across, in a line from one level to another.

  2. In the Geo tray, tick Obstacle or Impassable.

  3. Set Transition to Directional and toggle the directions along the bridge.

  4. Press Save to Squares.

A crossing can now leap along the bridge squares and land up to 8 squares away, on a different level from where it started. Units can't stop on the bridge itself (these squares are Obstacles or Impassable by necessity).

To link two teleporters

  1. Select exactly two squares, using Alt + drag for the second. Teleport Pair is only offered with two squares selected.

  2. In the Geo tray, set Transition to Teleport Pair.

  3. Give the pair a Tag of one or two letters. It's shown on the map, and reusing a tag moves it from its old squares.

  4. Set the Activation Cost: Standard Action ends the unit's turn, Bonus Action ends its movement, and Movement costs the Mov you enter and lets it keep moving.

  5. Tick Blockable? if an occupied far square should stop the teleport. Otherwise the unit arrives on the nearest free square. Type Restriction works here too.

  6. Press Save to Squares.

A unit teleports by ending a move on either square and confirming, whatever the height or distance between them. Outside combat it's free.

Objectives, Hazards and Reinforcements

To mark where units arrive or what they must hold

  1. Select the squares.

  2. In the Mech tray, set Objective Point to Arrival Point or Defense Point.

  3. Press Save to Squares.

  4. Switch to Settings mode and press Edit on the Objectives card to give the map an Arrive or Defend objective (see @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.fRmf6UOHviDS5kFI#setting-objectives]{Setting Objectives}).

The markers are always shown on the map, but do nothing unless the scene itself is enabled as a Defense or Arrival map via the 'Set Objectives' menu by the GM.

A player unit that ends its turn on an Arrival Point, or is standing on one when the Player Phase ends, has arrived and leaves the map. A Defend map is lost if an enemy is standing on a Defense Point at the end of the Enemy Phase.

To make a square heal or damage units

  1. Select the squares.

  2. In the Mech tray, press Add Effect Array under Tile Effect.

  3. Choose a Type, Healing or a damage type, and enter the Value.

  4. For Healing, enter the Stn restored. For damage, tick Can Kill PC if it may take a Lord or Retainer below 1 HP. Otherwise, automatic damage from these squares will never reduce a unit below 1 HP, similar to hazardous squares in FE.

  5. Press Save to Squares.

The effect applies to the unit standing on the square at the start of its side's phase. Healing comes first. Damage is only reduced by Def or Res if the unit's armor's Protections include that damage type.

Spawn Points

To bring in reinforcements

  1. Open the actor's sheet and press Copy Document UUID in its header. The actor can be in the world or a compendium.

  2. Select the square the unit should appear on.

  3. In the Mech tray, press Add Spawn Array under Spawn Unit, and paste into Actor UUID. The row takes the actor's name once it's found.

  4. Set Start Round, End Round and Cooldown Rounds. For one arrival, set Start Round and End Round to the same round.

  5. Choose a Spawned Unit Behavior if the Enemy AI module should drive the unit (see @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.4bL4mJsYfkVkFUxV]{Configuring Enemy AI}).

  6. Press Save to Squares.

A marker with the actor's token art in a gold ring appears in the corner of the square while the builder is open or Terrain Tips are on. Each array places one unit each time it fires, so add several arrays, or use several squares, for a group.
