When spawns happen. Spawns fire at the end of a phase, in the rounds their arrays allow: player-side units (Lords, Retainers and Allies) arrive at the end of the Player Phase, and everyone else at the end of the Enemy Phase. The spawned token is a new, unlinked copy of the actor, placed with its top-left corner on the spawn square. It fades in, and every player gets a ping on the map, with the camera panning there if it's off screen. Spawn history resets each time an encounter begins, and a spawn that's blocked tries again at its next chance.

Spawns and objectives. A Rout objective's Count spawned reinforcements option decides whether spawned enemies have to be defeated too. Objectives are checked before that phase's spawns arrive.

To exempt some units from a square's Effects

  1. Select the squares.

  2. In the Adv tray, press Add Exception.

  3. Choose Match By: Unit Type (such as Flying or Undead), Faction Type (Player, Enemy or Neutral), Name (the exact unit name) or Actor ID (the actor's UUID), and enter the Value.

  4. Under Sync, tick Move Cost and Tile Effect if the unit should ignore those too.

  5. Press Save to Squares.

A matching unit always ignores the square's Eva, Def and Res, and whatever you ticked under Sync. Exceptions never affect obstacles or transitions. The Ichorous Pool preset exempts Undead from all three.

What Terrain Overrides may do to a square

Some spells, abilities or bombs paint terrain of their own onto squares, like the Flasked Fire bomb setting them aflame. Overwrite Behavior in the Adv tray sets what happens to the square's own terrain:

  • None: the spell's terrain replaces the square's, and the original comes back when it ends.

  • Forbid Overwrite: spells can't change this square.

  • Clear: when the spell's terrain ends, the square is left bare, like a forest burnt away.

  • Clear with Respawn: the square is left bare for the set number of Rounds, then its original terrain comes back. It also comes back when the encounter ends.

Lights, Sounds and VFX

In each of these trays, a rectangle of squares normally gets one light, sound or effect per square. Tick Span Selection for one at the centre of the rectangle instead, or, for FX, one stretched across it.

To add a light

  1. Select the square, or a rectangle for one light at its centre.

  2. In the Light tray, set Dim Radius and Bright Radius in squares. One has to be above 0.

  3. Set Color, Color Intensity, Animation, and whether it's Constrained by Walls. The Advanced section holds Foundry's finer light options: animation speed and intensity, Provides Vision, coloration technique, luminosity, attenuation, saturation, contrast and shadows.

  4. Press Save to Squares.

The builder places a Foundry light for it, which Show Light Objects in the control group reveals.

To add an ambient sound

  1. Select the square, or a rectangle for one sound at its centre.

  2. In the Audio tray, enter the Sound File: a file path, or a Sequencer sound name.

  3. Set its Radius in squares (3 by default), Volume (0.8 by default) and Volume Easing.

  4. Press Save to Squares.

The sound loops. Walls don't block terrain sounds. Show Sound Objects in the control group reveals it.

To add a looping visual effect

This needs the Sequencer module. FX are only for show.

  1. Select the square, or a rectangle to stretch one effect across.

  2. In the FX tray, enter the Effect: a Sequencer database name, like jb2a.markers..., or a file path.

  3. Set Scale, Opacity, Rotation and Mirror X or Mirror Y.

  4. Press Save to Squares.

The effect plays under the tokens.

Drawing Walls

Draw Walls mode draws Foundry walls without leaving the builder. Doors aren't drawn here: a door in Emblem RPG is a Door Object, which walls itself off while it's closed (see the @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.rW7yhTmpFeEhmCby]{Objects page}).

  • Drawing Mode. Snap to Grid and Freestyle draw a wall by dragging; hold Alt to chain the next wall onto it. Freestyle lays a new wall every Bone Length pixels. Polygon places a point on each click; click the first point, press Enter or right-click to finish, and Esc to cancel. In any mode, right-click a wall to delete it.

  • Wall Type. Solid blocks movement, sight, light and sound. Terrain blocks movement, and sight, light and sound pass the first such wall. Invisible blocks movement only. Ethereal blocks sight and light only. Window blocks movement and sound, and sight and light pass within 2 squares. The Restrictions and Proximity Thresholds cards adjust the chosen type; a wall has to block movement or sight.

  • Scene Walls. Counts the scene's walls. Clear All Walls deletes every wall except those of Door Objects, after asking.

Scene Settings

The Settings mode holds options for the whole scene. Every change is saved as soon as you make it.

  • Combat Music. Player Phase Track and Enemy Phase Track set the playlist or single track played during each phase of an encounter on this map, when the combat tracker's Combat Music is on.

  • Movement Type Permissions. Allowed (default), No Flying (grounds every flier that isn't levitating) or No Mounts (prevents mounting and dismounts riders).

  • Move Scaling. Changes every unit's movement on this map: Slowed (-1, never below 1), None, Boosted (+1) or Accelerated (+2, or +3 when mounted).

  • Show grid in builder. Shows the builder's grid overlay, for your client only.

  • Vision & Fog. Token Vision, Global Illumination, Fog Exploration (Disabled, Individual or Shared) and Darkness are Foundry's own scene settings. Map Visible keeps fog of war but reveals the whole map as already explored, so players see the layout but only see units within sight. It turns on Token Vision and fog exploration.

  • Objectives. A summary of the map's win and loss conditions, with an Edit button that opens the objectives dialog.

Notes

  • Eva, Def and Res run from -10 to +10 and are added to the stats of a unit standing on the square. A unit covering several squares takes the best bonus and the worst penalty under it, not the total. Airborne units get none.

  • Move Cost runs from 0 to 10 and is 1 by default. 0 makes the square free to enter.

  • Obstacle: ground units can't enter. Fliers can cross it but not land on it; a flier knocked down onto one is stranded until it takes off. Impassable: no unit can enter, airborne or not. Fliers ignore every other terrain cost, stat and height.

  • The Overview tray. Shown for a single square with saved terrain, it lists everything the square carries. Click an entry to open the tray that sets it. Eva, Def, Res and Move can be edited right there, and clicking the Obstacle or Impassable chip turns that flag off.

  • Where It's Saved. Terrain, zones and objectives are saved on the scene. Your presets are in Data/worlds/<world>/json/terrain.json.

The Enemy AI module can play the Enemy Phase for you, moving and attacking with each Enemy, Boss and Neutral unit in turn. Turning it on during a map is covered under @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.fRmf6UOHviDS5kFI#enemy-automation]{Enemy Automation} on the Combat page. This page is about telling each unit how to play.

Every unit is set up in the Combat AI tab of its Actor Control Panel, marked with a brain icon and shown only to the GM. The tab applies to Enemy, Boss and Neutral units. Allied NPCs are currently meant to be controlled by the GM so that the player characters have the chance to coordinate with them (don't you hate how green units never do what you want in FE?). And obviously Retainers and Lords need no AI operations.

How Combat AI Works

  • A unit's Combat AI Profile is its temperament: how it weighs the damage it deals against the counterattack it takes, where it falls in the Enemy Phase order, and whether it falls back to recover when its Stance breaks. A new unit is Balanced.

  • Priority puts a unit ahead of the others in the Enemy Phase. Higher acts first; the default is 0. E.g. give a Boss Priority 5 and it moves before every rank-and-file unit, whatever their profiles say.

  • Conditions let a unit change its mind as the battle unfolds. Each entry pairs a Condition with a Behavior. At the start of its turn the unit checks its entries from top to bottom and follows the first one that holds; if none holds, it takes a normal turn under its profile.

  • A Behavior either changes how the unit moves when it has nothing to attack (Free Roam, Pursue, Seize), or replaces its turn (Retreat), or swaps its profile for the rest of the battle (Switch AI Profile).

  • The AI attacks with whatever weapons and attack spells a unit carries, but it uses other items only when they've been given a Role on the item's sheet. Right now the only role is Heal.

  • A unit set to Manual is yours. The AI pauses at its place in the order until you've played it and ended its turn.

Combat AI Profiles

The Combat AI Profiles available for you to play around with are:

  • Balanced. The default. Weighs the damage it deals against the counterattack it takes. Acts mid-phase, and falls back when its Stance breaks.

  • Cautious. Fears counterattacks, avoids squares enemies can hit from where they stand, seeks cover, and shuns hazards and risky Zone crossings. Acts late, and falls back when its Stance breaks.

  • Defensive. Like Cautious, but prizes defensive terrain and holds its ground. It never falls back.

  • Aggressive. All but ignores counterattacks, cover and small hazards, and hunts flanks hardest of any profile. Acts first, and never falls back.

  • Berserk. Attacks anything it can reach, even when the blow would do nothing, and ignores counterattacks and hazards. Acts first, and never falls back.

  • Support. Prefers healing wounded allies to attacking, using items given the Heal role. Otherwise plays like Cautious. Acts last, and falls back when its Stance breaks.

  • Passive. Does nothing and ends its turn at once, until a Switch AI Profile condition wakes it.

  • Manual. When the AI reaches a unit whose profile is set the 'Manual', it will pause itself. The GM will be notified to manually operate this unit's turn before the rest of the AI processing resumes.

  • Unpredictable. Plays as Cautious or Aggressive, rolled each round, acts at a random point in the phase, and flips a coin on falling back.

Turn Order. Units with a higher Priority act first. Among units of equal Priority, those whose attacks break Stance or apply a debuff go first, followed by the profile order above: Aggressive and Berserk, then Balanced and Manual, then Cautious and Defensive, then Support and Passive.

Falling Back. A Stance Broken unit whose profile falls back spends its turn moving away from its enemies, then ends its turn to recover its Stance, the same way a player would rest a broken unit.

Setting Up Units

To set a unit's profile

  1. Open the unit's character sheet and press Control Panel in its header.

  2. Open the Combat AI tab.

  3. Pick a Combat AI Profile.

  4. Set its Priority if it should act before or after the others.

The unit plays by that profile from its next Enemy Phase. With no conditions, the tab says so: the unit simply follows its profile.

To make a unit change its behavior mid-battle

Use this when a unit should hold still until something happens, chase the party once it has nothing in reach, or run when badly hurt.

  1. In the Combat AI tab, press Add Entry under Conditions.

  2. Pick the Condition: Always; Aggressed (a hostile unit attacked it, or used an item on it, since its last turn ended); HP <100%, <75%, <50% or <25%; Stance Broken; or At Round, which adds a From Round field and applies from that round onward.

  3. Pick the Behavior. Switch AI Profile adds Switch To, the profile to switch to. Free Roam and Pursue add Max Squares, the squares of movement to spend each turn, 0 for all of it.

  4. Add further entries, and put the most urgent at the top. Click an entry's header to fold it, and the bin icon to remove it.

Order matters, because only the first entry whose condition holds is followed. For instance, with HP <25%: Retreat above Always: Pursue, the unit chases until badly hurt, then flees. Once a unit has switched profile, its Switch AI Profile entries no longer count, so the entries below them still apply: At Round 3: Switch AI Profile (Aggressive) above Always: Pursue keeps a Passive unit still until round 3, after which it fights aggressively and chases when it has nothing in reach. A Manual unit's conditions are greyed out, since the AI never plays it.

To let the AI heal with an item

  1. Open the sheet of the item, which can be a consumable, an active ability, a utility spell or a utility staff, and press AI Parameters in its header.

  2. Set Role to Heal.

  3. Set Heal Below %, so the AI only heals allies below that share of their max HP, and Amount, the HP the item is expected to restore. The AI weighs that amount against attacking.

Give the unit the Support profile if healing should come first; any other profile heals only when it beats the attack on offer.
NOTE: The AI's ability to take actions other than attacking is currently limited to just this healing role. My plans are for the GM to eventually be able to configure actions and abilities which the AI will know how/when to use. For now, the scope of this functionality is limited to healing.

To Configure multiple units at once

  1. Select the tokens on the map.

  2. Run Configure Combat AI from the GM Macros compendium. The Set Combat AI on Selected window opens, filled in from the first selected unit.

  3. Tick Overwrite AI Profile to set the Combat AI Profile and Priority of every selected unit.

  4. Tick Overwrite Conditions to replace every selected unit's conditions with the list in the window. An empty list clears them. Units being set to Manual keep the conditions they have.

  5. Press Overwrite.

Behaviors

  • Switch AI Profile. The unit plays by the profile chosen under Switch To for the rest of the battle. The profile saved in the Control Panel doesn't change.

  • Retreat. The unit spends its whole turn moving as far as it can from the nearest enemy, and takes no action. If no square is further away, it stays where it is.

  • Free Roam. When the unit has nothing to attack, it wanders to a random square it can reach.

  • Pursue. When the unit has nothing to attack, it advances on the enemy it can reach soonest, by the route that best avoids danger. It keeps chasing the same target unless another becomes nearer by more than a turn's movement.

  • Seize. Before acting, the unit heads for the nearest Defense Point, breaking through a wall or attacking a unit in its way when that's quicker than going around. It still attacks along the way.

A Taunted unit, e.g. from the Threaten ability, chases its taunter instead of following any of these. A unit placed by a spawn point with a spawn behavior (Pursuant, Roaming or Seizing) is given that behavior as an Always entry at the bottom of its conditions (see @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.ZxXYJlf5ACElkTNj#spawn-points]{Spawn Points}). In the combat tracker, a footprints icon marks a unit currently following Pursue (red), Free Roam (yellow) or Seize (white). Only the GM sees it.

Notes

  • Hidden Tokens. The AI plays the enemy units that are alive and visible on the map. A hidden token (e.g. hidden via Foundry's native hide/show toggle) is treated as not having real existence on the map. The AI will ignore them.

  • Armaments. Currently, enemy AI is not able to operate Armament objects on a map, e.g. a Ballista. For now, if you want enemy units to use these field weapons, you must control them manually.

  • Neutral Units. Neutrals do not yet have a phase of their own, so the AI plays them during the Enemy Phase alongside Enemies and Bosses.

Every weapon, spell, ability, consumable and class in Emblem RPG is an Item, built on its item sheet and the editors the sheet opens. The GM, Assistant GMs, and Trusted Players who own an item can edit it. This page teaches the editors by building real items, from a plain weapon up to a bomb that sets the map on fire, and then lays out every field for reference.

Before you edit an item that came from an Emblem RPG compendium, duplicate it in your world first and edit the copy. The GM macro Synchronize World Content overwrites every world item whose ID is sourced from a compendium pack, and would wipe your changes. If you never run that macro you'll have no trouble, but it's also the only way to bring your other content up to date with the shipped content without reimporting it.

Item Sheet Documents

  • Type and subtype. Create Item in the Items directory asks for a type: Equipment, Consumable, Ability, Spell, Class, Miscellaneous or Resource. The selector at the top of the sheet then picks what it is. Equipment is a Weapon, Armor, Shield, Accessory, Staff, Staff (U) or Mount. A Consumable is a Potion, Bomb, Booster, Promotion, Coinpurse or Other. An Ability is Active, Passive or a Weapon Art. A Spell is Attack or Utility.

  • The sheet says what the item is. Its stats, uses, target, range and action type. The tabs are Overview, Effects, Modifiers and Requirements.

  • Effects say what it does. An Effect is a trigger plus a list of steps that run in order: deal damage, apply a status, move a unit, play an animation. An item can hold several, each on its own trigger. E.g. Flasked Fire has three: Activation paints fire onto the squares, Fail Save deals 2d12, Pass Save deals 1d12.

  • An Activation effect runs once per target. So a step aimed at self, or at an area, repeats for every unit the item catches. The editor warns you when that happens.

  • Modifiers are lasting changes to a unit's stats while it carries, wears or wields the item, like a ring that raises Spd. An Aura is a modifier that reaches units within range.

  • Requirements gate use. When one fails, the use is refused and the player is told which one.

  • Statuses are defined where they're applied. An Apply status step applies a stock status, or a custom one you build in the step itself.

  • Animations come in two places. Animation Settings on the sheet plays when the item is used, and an Animation step plays wherever you put it in an effect. Both run through the Sequencer module.

Sample Tutorials

Each one builds on the last. The bomb and the push ability rebuild shipped items, Flasked Fire and Shove, so you can open the originals and compare.

1. A Weapon

  1. Press Create Item in the Items directory, choose Equipment, and name it. On the sheet, set the subtype to Weapon.

  2. Set Proficiency to the weapon type, such as Blade, and the rank a unit needs to wield it, E to S.

  3. Fill in Atk, Brk, Rng (1, or a span like 1-2), Wgt, Acc and Crit. Set Hands (one handed or two handed) and the Atk Stat the weapon scales on: Might, Wit, or Hybrid. Hybrid will set the weapon to use Mgt when in melee range, and Wit otherwise (e.g. for a Levin Sword).

  4. Under Damage Types, tick the type(s) it deals, such as Slashing. A weapon can deal more than one. You can click the 'Damage Types' label itself to open an editor where you can establish conditions for when that Damage Type is available. For example, you might make a 'Fire Sword' that deals Slashing and Fire damage, but if you wanted the Fire damage to only apply at range, you would have to add a condition to it that checks 'inMeleeRange' as falsy.

  5. Set Durability to Limited with its maximum uses. Each landed blow costs one.

  6. If the weapon should be effective against a unit type, or beat a weapon type, tick it under Effective Type(s) or Weapon Breaker(s). Extra Attacks adds strikes per attack.

Later down this journal page, you will also find information detailing how to give the weapon Animation data, as well as Crafting data, in order to fully flesh it out.

2. A Bomb With a Saving Throw

This rebuilds Flasked Fire: thrown up to 5 squares, it sets the aimed square and the four beside it on fire for a phase and burns everything standing there, with a save for half.

The item

  1. Create a Consumable, set its subtype to Bomb, and name it.

  2. Set Action Type to Standard Action and Uses to 1, Limited.

  3. Click Target to open Target Parameters. Set target type Any, shape Location, grid colour Red, valid squares All, and tick unoccupied only.

  4. Set Range to 5 and Radius to 1. With the Cross shape, that's the aimed square plus one step up, down, left and right.

The save

  1. On the Effects tab, press Add Params.

  2. Set required check to Saving throw, base dc 8, caster adds Tqn, target rolls Agi. Each unit caught in the blast rolls Agi against 8 plus the thrower's Tqn.

The effects

  1. Press + Add Effect. Set the trigger to Activation and name it. Add an Edit terrain step: leave who at cast area, set phases to 1, tick overwrite, and pick the Flasked Fire tile preset. Save.

  2. Add a second effect on Fail Save. Add a Damage step: who target, amount 2d12, type Fire, stance damage 2, apply mitigation ticked.

  3. Add a third effect on Pass Save, with a Damage step of 1d12 Fire and no stance damage.

The Bomb's animation

  1. Press Animation Settings in the header. On the Adjacent tab, add a sound step for the throw, then an effect step with file jb2a.throwable.throw.bomb.01.black, at location token, stretch to target-location, scale 0.5, and wait until finished 200.

  2. Add an explosion sound, then an effect step with file jb2a.fireball.explosion.orange at location target-location, scale 0.4.

  3. Set the tab's duration to 1000, so the damage lands as the fireball blooms. Copy the steps and paste them onto the Ranged tab.

Give the bomb to a unit and throw it at an empty square beside two enemies. Both roll, the squares turn to fire, and the Overview tray in the Terrain Builder lists the bomb's terrain on each square with a phase left. To let it be crafted at a Laboratory, press Crafting Settings and set the skill check, difficulty class and required materials. To have it award XP, add it to the world's experience table (below).

3. A Personal Passive

A Passive ability sits in a unit's inventory and changes its stats through the Modifiers tab. The three below are the personal abilities suggested under Character Creation on the Getting Started page. Each starts the same way: create an Ability, set its subtype to Passive, name it, and open the Modifiers tab.

A flat XP bonus

  1. Press Add Modifier.

  2. Name it, set stat to XP Multiplier (%), and amount to 20. The stat starts at 100, so this is +20% XP.

  3. Leave only while equipped and only while active unticked, so it applies while the item sits in the inventory.

A bonus while injured

  1. Press Add Modifier. Name it, set stat to Attack and amount to 3.

  2. Open its condition. Press + rule, choose compare, type hp as the property, pick the < operator, and enter maxHp / 2 as an expression.

The +3 Atk now shows on the unit's sheet only while its HP is below half, like Bernadetta's personal skill.

A Retainer's aura for its Lord

An aura effect that reads: 'This unit grants +3 attack to their Lord while the two units are adjacent', would look like this:

  1. Tick Enable Aura and set Rng to 1.

  2. Press Add Modifier and choose the Aura Modifier. Set stat to Attack, amount 3, and applies to Friendly.

  3. Add a condition to that modifier which

Every friendly unit standing next to the Retainer gains +3 Atk. An aura amount has to be a plain number, and auras can't use only while equipped. Drag each finished passive onto its unit; passives work from the inventory with nothing to equip.

4. Berserk: a Self-Buff With a Custom Status

Berserk is an Active ability. As a Bonus Action, the unit gains +5 Atk and +10 Crit, but becomes vulnerable to every damage type and loses its protections, for 6 phases. Using Berserk while raging ends it early. Here's how you'd build it from scratch.

The item

  1. Create an Ability named Berserk and set its subtype to Active. Write its description.

  2. Set Target to Self.

  3. Set Uses to 1, Limited, and tick Refreshes, so the GM's Restore macros refill it between maps.

  4. On the Overview tab, set Action Type to Bonus Action and tick Retractable. The player can then take Berserk back before acting.

The effect

  1. On the Effects tab, press + Add Effect. Set the trigger to Activation, name it Berserk, and tick hold pose.

  2. Add an If step. In its condition, add a status rule: self has Berserk.

  3. In its then list, add a Remove status step: who self, which by name, status name Berserk, amount full removal, applied by self. This is the early ending.

  4. Press + else. In the else list, add an Animation step with wait until finished ticked, and press Edit Animation Steps: an effect step with file animated-spell-effects-cartoon.fire.15, at location token, layer aboveInterface, scale to token 2; a sound step with file blfx.sound.misc.explosion.fire.1; and a duration of 1000.

  5. Below the Animation step, still in the else list, add an Apply status step: who self, status custom, phases 6, reapplication renew duration.

Keep in mind that a second use needs a use left. With 1 use, Berserk can only be ended early after its uses are refilled, so an ability you want to toggle within one map needs more uses, or Infinite.

The status

In the Apply status step's custom status panel:

  1. Set name Berserk, an icon, id tag berserk-effect, and a description stating its effects.

  2. Leave polarity at neutral, so a step that removes all harmful or all beneficial statuses leaves it alone.

  3. Under ends when, tick phase begin and untick phase end. Applied during the unit's own phase, Berserk then lasts that phase and its next five.

  4. Leave stackable unticked.

  5. Add the changes:

    1. In the first field, it wants the path to the data point you want to alter.

    2. In the second field, 'how', select either add or override. The first option tells Foundry to treat this as an additive modifier, while the second option will replace the current value entirely with the new value given by the status effect.

    3. In the third field, 'value', enter the number to modify the attribute by (if add) or to (if override). For a boolean attribute, this will show up as simply true or false.

    4. In the forth field, 'priority', this tells Foundry how to prioritize this modifier if two modifiers exist targeting the same attribute, e.g. if two status effects both want to override a target's 'Infantry' unit type, then the effect with the higher priority wins out.

  6. For our 'Berserk' ability, all we need to do is add stats.atk.mod, how: add, value: 5, priority: 99, and do the same with stats.crit.mod, setting its value to 10. Then we add every single damage type in the game and override the unit's vulnerabilities to them as true, and protections from them as false.

The end result is a status effect, lasting 6 rounds, which gives the unit a big attack buff, but makes them deeply vulnerable to being Stance Broken.

5. Shove: A Push With a Skill Check and a Requirement

This rebuilds Shove. As a Bonus Action, the unit rolls Athletics against the target's Bld to push it one square away, but only against a unit of its own size.

  1. Create an Ability, subtype Active, named Shove. Set Action Type to Bonus Action and Uses to Infinite.

  2. Click Target: target type Any, shape Single, grid colour Purple. Set Range to 1.

  3. On the Effects tab, press Add Params. Set required check to Skill check, skill Athletics, base dc 3, target adds Bld, and tick friendlies auto-succeed, so an ally can be shoved without a roll.

  4. On the Requirements tab, press Add Activation Requirement, choose Condition, and name it Size Comparison. Add a truthy rule with the expression caster.size === target.size.

  5. Back on the Effects tab, add an effect on Pass Check. Its steps, in order: an Animation step (a punch sound, and an effect with file jb2a.impact.007.yellow at location target, scale to token 1); a Wait of 200 ms; a Move token step with who moves target, how push away, with self, distance 1.

  6. Add an effect on Fail Check with a Resist popup step on the target.

  7. In Animation Settings, tick skip cinematic on the Adjacent tab.

Shove now refuses a target of a different size with a notice naming the requirement, rolls Athletics against 3 plus the target's Bld, and on a pass knocks the target one square straight back. The Wait step is what lets the impact flash land before the token slides.

Authoring a Class

A Class item carries a unit's base stats, growths, limits, proficiencies, skills, features and promotion paths. Making one for a player's Lord is how you give them a unique starting class, as described under Character Creation on the Getting Started page.

To make a custom class

  1. Find the shipped class closest to what you want, such as Trainee, and duplicate it into the world. Or create a Class item and pick its tier: Novice, Intermediate, Advanced, Unplayable or Unique.

  2. Rename it and write its description.

  3. Under Proficiencies, click a proficiency to step its rank. Click a Unit Type to toggle it.

  4. Under Skills, click a skill to step its die.

  5. Fill in Base Stats, Stat Growths and Stat Limits. A limit left blank is no limit.

  6. Under Features, press the add button for a bundle. Set its level and acquisition type.

    1. All grants every feature in the bundle the moment its designated Level is met by the unit

    2. Choice lets the player pick the number under choices. Search for each feature and click it to add it.

    3. Tick Unique for features that are lost on promotion, and list the classes that keep them under exceptions.

  7. Under Promotions, press the add button for a path. Set Req Level to designate the required level the unit must be before they can promote into that Class, drop the Promotion Item that unlocks it, search for the class it leads to, and click any Required Weapon Proficiencies and Required Skill Ranks.

To put the class on a unit, open its character sheet and press the magnifying-glass button beside the class name. The list offers every Class in the world and its compendiums, plus a blank class per tier, and the one you pick is copied onto the unit. A player's extra growth points go on the character sheet itself, by right-clicking the stat, not on the class, or they'll vanish at promotion.

BalaNCing a Custom Class

The best way to go about this is just to look at what already exists, and double check that your custom class's stats, growth rates, and stat limits aren't on average, too much higher or lower. Typically, most classes will get a new feature or feature bundle at levels 1, 3 and 5 for a Novice class, and 7, 9, 13 and 17 for an Intermediate unit. The exceptions are classes like Wyverner or Wingrider, who lose out on one of these threshold features because they make up for it by having flying mounts. Think about the give-and-take, using the existing classes as a reference. For instance, suppose you want to make a Knight (a cavalier) with more abilities than normal. Alright—what do you give? If you give them an extra ability at Lv 15 that the reference class doesn't have, then what are they losing in exchange?

Modifiers, requirements, damage types and the Effect editor's If steps all share one condition builder. A condition is a group of rules joined by and or or; + rule adds a rule and + group a nested group. Each rule is one of:

  • truthy. A property that is truthy or falsy.

  • status. Self or target has, or does not have, a named status.

  • chance (Effect editor only). A percent chance.

Typing in a property field opens a searchable list of properties, grouped as Life, Stats, Unit type, Status, Gear and so on. A plain property reads the item's own unit; prefix it with target. to read the other unit, as in target.hp. Experience Data

Items that are used outside an attack exchange, such as healing spells, bombs and curses, give XP only if they have an entry in the world's experience table: Data/worlds/<world>/json/exp-data.json. The system copies the default table there the first time the world loads. You can edit the file to change existing awards, or to give XP to your own custom items; every client then needs to reload for the changes to take effect. For how combat XP works, see @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.EKqsPYVWwd9HQqoq#experience]{Experience}.

{
  "items": {
    "Salve, Grace, Staff of Healing": { "exp-mode": "damage-based", "target-mode": "single", "leveled": true, "value": 30, "min": 2, "max": 30 },
    "Fireball": { "exp-mode": "damage-based", "target-mode": "multiple", "value": 50, "leveled": true, "max": 50, "kill-bonus": true },
    "Empower": { "exp-mode": "flat", "target-mode": "single", "value": 5, "limit": 10 }
  }
}

Each key under items names one or more items, separated by commas. Names must match the item's name, though capitals don't matter. If a name appears twice, the later entry is used. Each entry takes these fields:

  • exp-mode (required). How the award is worked out: flat, the value on every use; pass-fail, the value for each target the item affected, such as an enemy that failed its save or an ally that received a buff; damage-based, the value times the share of each target's max HP and max Stn the item dealt or restored. Healing 90% of an ally's max HP counts as a full heal.

  • value (required). The base XP, a number of 0 or more.

  • target-mode. single counts only the best-scoring target; multiple adds every target together. Defaults to single.

  • leveled. When true, each target's XP scales with its level against the user's: none for a target 5 or more levels lower, double for one 5 or more levels higher. Defaults to false.

  • min and max. The least and most XP one use can give. min is given even when no target counted. Defaults to 0 and no maximum.

  • limit. How many uses per encounter give XP. Defaults to no limit.

  • kill-bonus. When true, each enemy the item defeats also gives the normal combat XP for a defeat. Defaults to false.

Experience from items is only given during an encounter, and it is scaled by the unit's XP % and the world's XP multiplier like any other XP. An entry with an invalid field is skipped with a warning. If the whole file can't be read, the system uses the default table. Deleting the file restores the defaults on the next load.

Rule of Cool

The freedom of Emblem RPG being a virtual table top ought to be exploited. Characters have the means to make Skill Checks for a reason. Always feel free to inject a bit of organic storytelling into your games by letting players do things via impromptu Skill Checks during combat or free exploration, so long as the moment calls for it. A prayer for divine intervention at a moment of dire straits? Roll Esoteric! Want to intimidate an injured foe into laying down their arms and fleeing? Roll Command. Stuff like this can only emerge through embracing the RP in TTRPG and can't always be captured by strict gamey mechanics. However much you want to embrace this, and what effects the players' can inject into the game this way, or how often they are able to do so, are ultimately between you and your table.

Awarding Character Interactions

While there are gameified ways of earning Support XP between characters, the GM ought to reward strong and compelling RP between Lords/Retainers as well in the form of granting Support XP between them. This can be given by adding a new Support on a unit's character sheet, or right clicking an existing support. The system will automatically apply the same amount granted to the partner. I recommend awarding 5 Support XP for more general RP, and anywhere from 10-20 XP for more compelling scenes. Truly engaging, dramatic moments might warrant a whole Rank increase, but that is up for you to decide as GM.

Roleplaying As Retainers

Depending on your players, this may go over better or worse. For Support conversations or scenes between Retainers themselves, which do not involve any player Lord character, it would not be compelling (I think) to have the GM speaking to themselves as both Retainers. Therefore, it falls on the player's responsibility to roleplay as their own Retainer for a scene. Two players may even find themselves RPing as two different Retainers, leaving the GM out of account. The ownership of a Retainer's personality therefore falls on both the player who owns the unit, and the GM.

This may get some getting used to, and remains optional, but it's worth challenging your players to try and embrace this. Before the Player engages with this, however, it is best for that Retainer's personality to already be well established in the campaign, and for the player to have a pretty good understanding of that character from the GM. While RPing as a Retainer, the player is more so taking on an acting role, following an invisible script of what that Retainer is outside of the player's fiat. While a player always has full control over how they want to RP and direct their Lord (their PC), they ought to stick within constraints of what their Retainer would say or would do, and the GM has final say about what is canonical about Retainers.

Object Actor Documents

An Object is an actor for anything on the map that isn't a unit: barricades, siege weapons, doors, chests, loot, and the stations your party uses in Downtime. Create one from the Actors directory as an Object, then choose its Type on the sheet. Choosing a type gives the Object default art and shows that type's settings.

The Object Sheet

Every Object sheet has the same header:

  • Portrait and name. Click the portrait to change the Object's image.

  • Type. Grouped as Map Structures (Destructible, Armament, Door), Lootables (Chest, Loot, Gathering Node) and Downtime Furnishings (Altar, Cooking Pot, Stationary, Workshop, Laboratory, Instrument).

  • Link. Links the token to the actor, so every placed copy shares one set of data. Leave it unticked for an Object you place many times, like a common door, so each copy keeps its own state.

  • Size. The token's width and height in squares, in steps of 0.5.

  • Image scale and Token tint.

An Object with no type (--) is plain scenery. It blocks ground units, lets fliers pass, and does nothing when a unit interacts with it.

Destructibles, Doors and Chests have two art states in place of a single image scale: Intact and Destroyed, or Closed and Opened. Each state row sets its own image, scale, tint and x/y offset in pixels, and the token switches art when its state changes.

Cutting Art From the Scene

Each art state row has a Cut From Scene button, for the GM only, which needs the Emblem RPG Studio module. It cuts a region of the scene's own artwork into an image for that state, so a wall or gate that's painted into your map can become an Object.

Objects on the Map

  • Objects never take a turn and have no vision. Their tokens are always drawn beneath units.

  • A unit uses an Object by standing on it and pressing Interact (default F). Doors are the exception: they're opened from a square beside them.

Destructible

A breakable obstacle, like a barricade, a cracked wall or a gate, that blocks the way until units break it.

  • Integrity. Current and maximum. Integrity is the Destructible's only health.

  • Block Flyers? Stops flying units passing over it while it stands.

Any unit can strike a Destructible, whatever its faction, with an attack or a damaging spell or item. Other items can't target it, and it can't be healed. Attacks deal it no HP damage: only Brk lowers its Integrity, adjusted by its vulnerabilities, protections and immunities the same way a unit's Stance is (see @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.fRmf6UOHviDS5kFI#stance-mechanics]{Stance Mechanics}). A Destructible never counterattacks, can't be critically hit, and grants no XP.

At 0 Integrity, it bursts into smoke and switches to its Destroyed art. The token stays on the map, but it no longer blocks movement and can't be targeted. Raising its Integrity on the sheet restores it, and placing an unlinked copy fills its Integrity to maximum.

Enemy units with the Seize behaviour break through a visible Destructible that blocks their path; other enemies ignore Destructibles. Use them to hold a chokepoint, guard an objective, or hide a shortcut the party can open up.

Armament

A fixed weapon, like a ballista, that a qualified unit can man during an encounter.

To man it, a unit stands on it and presses Interact. The unit can't be mounted, has to hold the required proficiency rank, and the Armament needs durability left. The unit sets down its own weapon, and attack targeting opens with the Armament as its weapon. Cancelling the targeting or stepping off the Armament hands it back and re-equips the unit's weapon. While manning it, the unit can't counterattack, and a flier that fires it lands.

Door

A barrier that blocks movement and sight until it's opened.

  • Key slot. Drag in the item that opens it: Equipment, a Consumable or a Miscellaneous item. The × clears it.

  • Lock toggle. Closed (blocks movement) or Open (passable).

A unit opens it from a square directly beside it (not diagonal) that can see it: press Interact, then click the door. A unit carrying the key is offered it first, and the key is used up. Otherwise, a unit with the Locktouch compendium ability can pick it.

Locked doors and chests can be opened in Exploration Mode as well, but at the cost of Energy. This is explained in the @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.sYye0P93AGik9kMZ#chests/locks]{Downtime page}.

Players can't close a Door once it's open; the GM closes it again with the lock toggle. A Door with no key and a DC of 0 only opens when you toggle it, which is handy for doors that open on a story event or an objective.

Chest

A container of items, optionally locked.

  • Key slot and DC. As on a Door.

  • Lock toggle. Locked or Unlocked.

  • Contents. Drag in Equipment, Consumables, Miscellaneous items and Resources. A Resource asks for an amount, and stacks.

  • Closed and Opened Token Src. An open chest image is set by default.

A unit stands on the chest and presses Interact. A locked chest has to be opened first; an unlocked one shows its contents. Units can also stow their own items in a chest. An emptied chest stays on the map. Loot

A pile of items on the ground that any unit can take.

The sheet only holds a Contents list, filled the same way as a Chest's. A unit stands on the pile and presses Interact to take what it wants; items can't be put back. A Loot pile you place yourself stays on the map when it's emptied.

The system also makes Loot piles on its own: when a defeated unit drops items (see @UUID[Compendium.emblem-rpg.game-manual.JournalEntry.IVQAFxldbOBazi4p.JournalEntryPage.fRmf6UOHviDS5kFI#placing-drops-or-loot]{Placing Drops or Loot}), and when a unit chooses Drop on the Ground for an item. Items dropped on a square that already has a pile join it. These piles are removed once they're emptied.
